speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is rather a difficult matter to get out a schedule of prices week by week governing the sale price of these articles. I still believe that the regulations which have been promulgated, if enforced, will bring the relief that iis desired. Of course, they will not make up the deficiency in the quantity of the feeds we have been discussing, for there has undoubtedly -been a great shortage. But, so far as- controlling the price is- concerned, I believe the regulations will be effective. Not very long ago, in one of the counties of western Ontario- I believe the case was mentioned in a return brought -down the other day-a prosecution was entered against a local miller by the president of a co-operative farmers' society, and a conviction secured, and on the word of the president of that society the prosecution succeeded in remedying the conditions in the county in which he lived.

I desire very briefly to make a few observations, but not by way of criticism of the introduction of oleomargarine into this country, for the Government are in the favoured position of having all the criticism come from their followers. My hon. friend from 'East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) in introducing this resolution took very great care to clear the previous Minister of Agriculture and -also the present minister from all responsibility for the Order in Council admitting oleomargarine free into this country, and he seemed to make out a case that was satisfactory to those who supported him. He put all the blame on the food controller, and the thought occurred to us on this side of the House, as it must have occurred to hon. gentlemen opposite. Who is looking after the rights of the agricultural

interests of this country? If neither the previous Minister of Agriculture nor the present Minister of Agriculture is responsible, which one of the twenty-three Cabinet ministers to whom we are paying salaries is safeguarding the country's dairying interest? I leave that thought with the minister in the hope that upon some future occasion he may be able to explain it satisfactorily to the electors. My hon. friend from East Lambton then proceeded to find all manner of fault with the administration of the regulations, and he was followed during the afternoon by other supporters of the Government all condemning the administration of the regulations; so I will leave that to hon. gentlemen opposite.
My hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) made the statement that throughout this country cheeise and butter factories were being put out of business, but he did not go to the root of the trouble and say why they were being put out of business. That story goes back as far as 1911, when, by virtue of a trade arrangement with the United States, we could have had free entry for our butter, milk and cream, and milk -and cream products, to the markets of the United States. The people of Canada refused to accept that proposal, so in 1913 the United States revised their tariff along lines to suit their own people. They said, "If you don't want to trade with us on the basis of the proposed arrangement of 1911, we are going to fix the tariff to suit ourselves and ourselves only." And they proceeded to put milk -and cream on the free list. The result of that legislation was that milk and cream from border towns and counties in Canada immediately began going to the United States.

For how long? Not more than six months anyway.
Mr.ROBB: It is going there still. Farmers in the county of Huntingdon are shipping milk to the United States to-day because they can get $3 a hundred there as compared with $2.70 in Canada. The result has been that the butter and cheese factories of the western part of the province of Quebec, at all events, have been shut down, and there is consequently a smaller production of butter and cheese in that section.
There was one feature which, so far as I could observe, the minister dodged very cleverly this evening. He did not attempt to explain to the House why we allow oleomargarine to come into this country free of duty when we place a tax upon butter, and

I think the people of this country are entitled to an explanation of that point. Furthermore, I am told that by virtue of some arrangement oleomargarine does not come into this country as freely as people are led to believe, and that its manufacture in Canada is limited to two big companies which have a considerable pull with this Government. I am not going to name them, for I think all hon. gentlemen know who they are. That is also something about which the people of this country will require an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture.
This afternoon several hon. gentlemen opposite in turn, claimed that their part of the country was the best dairying county in Canada. I thought that a little strange, especially on the part of my hon. friends from Ontario, because I had under my hand the prize list of the Toronto Exhibition, which shows that nearly all the prizes for butter went to the province of Quebec, and a few to the province of Manitoba. I might as well put the list on Hansard, so that my hon. friends from Ontario, when they want to buy good butter, will know where to go. The Journal of Agriculture states that in the class for creamery butter, in salted solids, Joseph Dansereau, of Verclieres, carried off the first prize with a score of 97; the second, third and fourth prizes in the salted class also went to Quebec. In the unsalted class, Quebec wfas again first, Achille Fournier, of Gentilly, scoring 97 points. In this class a Manitoba exhibitor took the third prize. The Challenge Trophy for the highest score for creamery butter on exhibition was also won by Achille Fournier, of Gentilly.
We w.ill leave that feature of it and refer to the closing remarks of the hon. Minister of Agriculture in reply to the hon. gentleman from East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) about the price of bran and shorts. The history of the fixing of the price of bran and shorts is perhaps not now known to all hon. gentlemen in this House. I got it first hand from a gentleman who was present at the fixing of the prices, and that gentleman is a supporter of the Conservative party, and, I believe, contributes largely to the campaign funds.

There is no such
party.

We'll not now, but there
was onoe. Whan they came together to fix the price it was proposed they should fix it at 824 a ton in bulk, but some said:
Why fix this price in bulk; the trade is accustomed to buying in bags and why not fix the price, bags included, so that people will know the cost? They said:	We are
getting near a general election and it would look better to fix it in bulk because it would be $24 instead of 830. And they fixed it at $24, to look better. That is the history of it, and the price was not long fixed when the friends of the Minister of Agriculture on the Food Control Board who fixed the price down low, and took good care that they should keep all the bran and shorts in western Canada, and 'a member of the Food Control Board absolutely prohibited the mills of western Canada shipping to eastern Canada. That is the simple story, which explains why we have a shortage of (bran and shorts in eastern Canada. They fixed the price low and kept it all to themselves. I have the evidence here, and will be glad to show it to the Minister of Agriculture. I think I can satisfy him that it is correct. I submit, however, to the hon. minister that that is not a fair way of treating the dairy interests. The hon. member for East Lamlbton (Mr. Armstrong) complains of the lax administration of the oleomargarine regulations. As a member of a dairy constituency, 1 submit that the hon. minister is not dealing quite fairly with the dairymen and the stock raisers of eastern Canada in attempting to fix the price of these foodstuffs away down low, and keep them all for western Canada. We are all one country, and we know that the people of western Canada are desirous of promoting the stock industry. I know that the province of Manitoba has made progress in recent years along the line of the dairy industry, but I ask the Minister of Agriculture if it is fair to expect the people of eastern Canada to eat the flour, that tney in western Canada may have cheap bran and shorts. Let me remind him that, according to regulations fixed by himself, you only get 26 bags of bran for every 74 bags of flour. That is important. You cannot run a flour mill unless you sell your flour, and it is eastern Canada that eats that flour. Is it fair that we should be asked to pay the high price for flour and get none of the 'bran and shorts? I leave these thoughts for the consideration of the Minister of Agriculture, in the hope that as Minister of Agriculture for all Canada he will take a broader view of it, and not attempt to narrow things down. Sure, they are.

That, in the opinion of this House, the present inadequate coal supply in Canada makes it imperative on the part of the Government to take immediate action with a view to prevent the possibility of any fuel shortage during next winter season.
He said: Mr. Speaker, bn many occasions during the twenty-two years that I have had the honour to sit in this Parliament, stock has been taken of our natural resources, but I must say that the speeches which tvere delivered on those occasions were more of an academic than of a practical nature. Last year my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) moved a resolution on the very subject which I intend to discuss this evening. His speech on that resolution was supported by statistics and by most valuable information. This year, I do not wish to steal a march on that hon. gentleman, although he has a motion on the Order Paper in regard to the question of coal. But as I do regard the present situation as most serious, I would like to test the views of the Government on the present fuel shortage in Canada.
We have just passed through a very severe winter, and we know now what troubles are ahead of us if we do not at the present moment take stock of our situation as regards coal and if we do not foresee the consequences attendant upon a further shortage. I must say first, Mr. Speaker, that I was pleased to learn of the appointment of Mr. C. A. Magrath as fuel controller for Canada. Every body regards Mr. Magrath as a most deserving and con-

scientious official, and I believe that during the few months he has held that office he has made good. I noticed the other day a press despatch from Washington, dated March 23rd, stating that Mr. Magrath had obtained some very valuable concessions from the American Government. By arrangement with the United States Fuel Administration, he has been granted for Canada a considerable tonnage, and he has the privilege, for the period mentioned in the order, of calling upon the Fuel Administration in the United States to issue permits to any shippers who apply to him; and it is stated further in the despatch that allotments of coal to Canada during the past season were made upon the same basis as if Canada had been one of the states of the Union. This expresses a splendid sentiment towards Canada on the part of the United States Government, and we are all pleased that Mr. Magrath has been able to obtain such excellent results. But, Mr. Speaker, we had very, very trying times last winter in our country. We had heatless days, a condition unknown in Canada before last winter. I happened to be in New York on the 31st December last, and when I saw so many large skyscrapers absolutely closed, and when, reading the New York Post on my way home, I learned that during that day in twelve hours eleven persons in that large and enterprising city had died of exposure because of the coal shortage, the shortage toeing caused partly by railway congestion and partly toy scarcity of labour, it dawned upon me that we in Canada were exposed to hours of great anxiety in the near future. As we are in a large degree dependent upon the United States for coal, especially we of the provinces of Ontario and Quelbec, it seems to me that it is the paramount duty of the Dominion Government to provide for future emergencies. Now that the winter is over is the time for the Government to really govern, (because to govern means to foresee. My resolution, I am pleased to say, is not presented in any carping or hostile spirit; I simply want some information from the Government.
Two days ago I noticed in the press that the United States Government had taken very stringent measures for the coming season. And we must remember that it is from the United States that we import such large quantities of bituminous and anthracite coal yet necessary. The coal business in the United States is now under the exclusive control of the Federal Government, so that there will be no more price pirating; the selling agent is to be forced out;
licenses are to be issued, and coal zones are being created within which the distribution of coal will toe localized. This is a very drastic measure. As regards our dependence on the United States with regard to fuel generally, let me say what, after all, is a truism, that we are practically at the mercy of any strike in the American coal mining districts or any industrial disorganization in the United States over which we have absolutely no control. A coal or railway strike in that country would seriously, if not fatally, affect the Dominion of Canada. But leaving aside the matter of labour conditions in the United States, there is another eventuality which we must face. The coal fields of that country are far from being inexhaustible, and the time may come when the American Government will put an embargo on the export of coal. In 1908, when President Roosevelt convened at Washington a meeting of the Governors of the various States and some of the leading officials and industrial experts of the Union, he used the following language:
This nation-
His words apply to Canada as well.
This nation began with the belief that its landed possessions were illimitable and capable of supporting all the people who might care to make our country their home; but already the limit of unsettled land is in sight, and, indeed, but little land fitted for agriculture now remains unoccupied save what can be reclaimed by irrigation and drainage. We began with an unapproachable heritage of forests; more than half of the timber is gone.
And, Mr. Speaker, he added the following ominous words:
We began with coal fields more extensive than those of any other nation and with iron ores regarded as inexhaustible, and many experts now declare that the end of both iron and coal is in sight. The enormous stores of minerals, oils and gas are largely gone.
This warning of the ex-Preeident to the Governors of the various states of the Union brought into existence the Conservation Commission of the United States, and, indirectly, by reaction, the 'Conservation Commission of Canada. I need not dilate on the beneficial effects of the conservation of natural resources or the splendid work done by our Conservation Commission. But we are nevertheless facing a very serious problem-that of coal shortage. Apart from food, raiment and shelter, nothing is so necessary or so essential as fuel for the maintenance of life and for the (carrying on of commerce and transportation. Though we are not dependent on the United States for our entire fuel supply, we must obtain

from them fifty-five per cent of our coal requirements. This is a matter of grave import, as artificial heat must he supplied in this country during seven or eight months of the year, if only for the purpose of maintaining life.
Let us see in just a few sentences what are the present fuel requirements of Canada. I (borrow my figures from a very interesting paper read (before the Mining Engineers' Association in Montreal a few weeks ago by Dr. Haanel, one of our officials here. In 1916, nearly 30,000,000 tons of coal, 299,426,121 imperial gallons of crude and refined oil products, and firewood valued ait aJbout $60,000,000 were required in Canada. During that year the railways burned 9,000,000,000 tons of bituminous coal; 7,000,000 tons were required for generating power and a large quantity was used for town gas, heating large (buildings, and manufacturing feoke. Anthracite coal to the amount of 4,000,000 tons was burned in domestic and1 other heating plants and for industrial purposes. In normal times, however, anthracite is largely used for heating purposes. Compared with these fuel requirements of Canada, what was the production of fuel in thie country during the same year? In 1916, 14,483,395 tons of (bituminous coal were produced in Canada, of which we exported 2,135,359 tons. Canada produced 6,934,288 imperial gallons of crude oil, and wood, fuel was burned to the value of approximately $60,000,000. So that- to meet our requirements it was necessary to import 17,580,603 tons of coal and 292,426,100 imperial gallons of crude and refined oil product. This indicates the extent of our dependence on the United States for these essential commodities.
I said a moment ago that the coal fields in the United 'States are not inexhaustible, and I quoted the words of President Roosevelt in 1908, at the time of the creation of the American Conservation Commission. I have, in the report of our Commission of Conservation of 1917, the opinion of a gentleman well known in Canada, Mr. W. J. Dick, mining engineer, which confirms the assertion made by President Roosevelt. Mr Dick, in a paper on problems relating to the mining industry of Canada says:
The supply of anthracite coal in the United States is limited and there is no assurance that its export to Canada will be long continued. In 1913, it was estimated that there were 16,153,000,000 tons of anthracite coal in the United States. In 1913, 91,524,922 tons were mined and, as it has been estimated that for every ton of coal lost, a ton and a half of coal is sold or used, the exhaustion is proceeding at the rate of over 152,000,000 tons per annum.
If production continued at the same rate, it [Mr. l.omieux. J
would exhaust the anthracite of the United States in little over 100 years. We must, therefore, expect that the price will gradually increase. Coincidentally with the rise in price, production will decrease, thus prolonging the life of the mines.
We have here confirmation of the words uttered in 1908 toy President Roosevelt. Mr. Dick predicts that within a century there will toe no more anthracite coal mined or exported from the United States. Canada has seventeen per cent of the world's coal reserve. Yet our production is relatively small. We import more than we produce. Are such conditions to remain as they are, or must they not be changed? T do not wish to weary the House with any statistics because they can toe found in any blue-book. Suffice it to s.ay that the fuel resources of Canada exist in the vast coalfields of the extreme eastern and western portions of Canada, in the lignite fields of the western provinces, in the natural gas fields of western Canada and Ontario, in the petroleum oil fields of Ontario, in the oil shales of New (Brunswick and Nova Scot!a, in the standing forests, and, finally, in the peat bogs in great areas, chiefly in central Canada. As to the distribution of our fuel resources, there are four classical districts, if I may so speak, each of which has an abundance of fuel peculiar to its own area. The first district is that portion of western Canada which can be economically supplied with bituminous and anthracite coal. The second district is that portion that can he supplied with lignite. The fourth district is that portion which is richly served by Nova Scotia coal. But the third district cannot be supplied with the above co-als; it must thus-be dependent upon the United States, or must develop and utilize its excellent peat bogs, and this is the case of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. What shall we do? Here are, in my humble judgment, some of the remedies that suggest themselves. First, we can proceed-and I am speaking by the book, because I have read some literature on the subject in the Commission of Conservation report and in some of the papers which have been read lately before the Institute of Mining Engineers-with the intensive exploitation of our peat hogs. In yesterday's Globe, I find that a special committee was appointed by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to study that phase of the subject of fuel supply. I find here, summed up, the estimated peat resources of Canada:
The engineers of the Department of Mines entertain no doubt as to the enormous extent of our peat deposits.

Seven bogs within convenient shipping distances of Toronto are estimated to be capable of producing approximately 26,500,000 tons of fuel; and seven bogs in the vicinity of Montreal could supply that city with 23,500,000 tons of fuel.	*
Five bogs along thfe lower St. Lawrence, conveniently situated as regards water transportation to the city of Quebec, can, it is estimated, supply 16,250,000 tons of fuel and 5,700,000 tons of peat litter.
The bogs examined in Nova Scotia can produce 6,200,000 tons of fuel and 500,000 tons of peat litter, and those of Prince Edward Island can produce, 1,250,000 tons of fuel and over 1,000,000 tons of peat litter.
In Manitoba the aggregate fuel contents of the bogs is estimated at less than 2,000,000 tons. One bog alone, however, it has been estimated, is capable of furnishing 2,500,000 tons of peat litter.
Dr. Haanel, who is our great expert, speaking on the economical operation and utilization of our peat hogs-I do not wish to inflict on the House the reading of all his suggestions, but I may be pardoned if I just give a few lines-says:
The only economic process in existence to-day-
That is, in order to utilize economically the peat bogs.
-is that which employs the forces of nature -the sun and the wind-for the removal of the moisture. The process employing these forces is called the "wet process," and the product obtained is termed "machine peat." This is the process which the Mines Branch, Department of Mines, demonstrated at the Government peat plant at Alfred, Ontario. We not only have the process for manufacturing peat fuel, but also sufficient detailed information concerning peat bogs of immediate importance, to make a good start in the formation of a peat industry. During the period covering the past ten years, the Mines Branch has completely investigated' and mapped 58 Canadian bogs, all of which are situated conveniently with respect to inhabited and industrial communities, and also well situated with respect to railway and other transportation facilities.
He concludes by saying:
Excellent bogs are likewise conveniently situated with respect to thickly inhabited communities in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and other parts of Canada.
After describing tihe rich peait bogs of Central Canada he advises that the Government should take the matter in hand at the earliest opportunity in order that this fuel may be utilized.
iHe says:
Not* until the utilization of a natural substance is forced by absolute necessity will the most sincere and earnest efforts be put forth to successfully and economically convert it into a usable product. It appears to me the time is at hand wben necessity will decide that we Canadians utilize our peat resources, and in the most efficient manner.
There the alarm bell is sounded, and the Government should pay heed to the advice given by this well-known expert and start in at once to utilize our peat bogs. Another course which suggests itself for the utilization of our resources against the eventuality of an embargo on coal from the United States is the treatment of lignite, which is found m such large beds all over the province of Saskatchewan. Mr. Haanel deals with this question also in his pamphlet. He says:	-
The utilization of certain of the lignites for some purposes is possible without any subsequent treatment. With others, notably those of Saskatchewan, the lignites as mined are not suitable for use. This is due to the physical and chemical properties peculiar -to this type of fuel. The characteristics of lignites must be altered before they can be converted into a satisfactory fuel. Experiments on a commercial scale have demonstrated beyond a doubt that our lignites cannot be briquetted in the raw state without the addition of a binder. Briquettes made in this manner appear on casual examination to be entirely satisfactory, but when submitted to a water test or when burnt they will invariably disintegrate. The establishment of briquetting plants at strategic points throughout the lignite provinces of the west would very greatly help in reducing our dependency for fuels upon other sources. While the domestic fuel is of course of first importance, lignite briquetting industries would prove also of great value to the railways traversing the lignite belts. It would even be within the realm of possibility to economically supply at least a portion of the province of Ontario with this class of fuel.
Another remedy wihieh suggests itself in the way of more intense production is the development of our oil resources. Professor Haanel in this paper says:
Our domestic production of oil cannot be increased without great effort and the expenditure of considerable money, but provision must be made, and immediately to provide against the time not far distant, when the United States will be compelled to cease exporting her crude and refined oil products.
I have already said (that Mr. Roosevelt, backed by Mr. Dick, has stated that within a hundred years there will be no more anthracite coal mined in .the United States, and therefore no more anthracite coal to export, and Mir. Haanel now states that within 30 or 35 years no more oil will be exported from the United States ; which means we must tap our own resources and develop them as economically as possible. Mr. Haanel says:
The United States up to the year 1915 had exhausted 32 per cent of her possible petroleum resources. If the present annual production is maintained, but not increased, her total crude oil supplies will be exhausted in less than thirty years. But if the present rate of increase of production is maintained, total exhaustion will occur in a much shorter time.

With regard to oil possibilities in Canada he says:
We can scarcely hope for some time to come to produce oil on a scale comparable with our demands, but we can appreciably reduce the quantity which must be imported. Our total oil production from all sources might probably be increased to 120,000,000 gallons, by erecting oil shale distillation plants in New Brunswick, with a combined capacity of 100,000,000 gallons and by increasing the quantity of coal coked in by-product ovens or by carbonizing large quantities of bituminous coal at low temperature, and briquetting the carbonized residue. The low temperature carbonization and briquetting of Nova Scotia coal either in Nova Scotia or at some centre of distribution favourably situated1 with respect to water transportation, as Montreal, for example, would not only appreciably increase our production of oils but would also be the means of supplying for domestic purposes a coal equal in many respects to anthracite. The fuel situation of some parts at least of Ontario might in this manner be much improved. If this idea were carried out our oil production would be: From oil shales 100,000,000 gallons ; from coke ovens and low temperature carbonization 14,000,000 gallons, and from Ontario petroleum fields 6,000,000 gallons, making a total of 120,0<00,000 gallons.
We icould .also (help to alleviate the present fuel shortage by developing our water-powers .and our hydro-electric energy. I do not wish to bore the House with this question, as we shall hear about hydroelectric energy in the course of this Session, but perhaps I might be permitted to remind my hon. friends that Mr. Roosevelt has sounded the alarm not only with regard to the ooal fields of the United States, hut also with regard to the water-powers, and his words apply 'equally to the waiter-powers of Canada.
Mr. Roosevelt said:
The people of this country are threatened by a monopoly far more powerful, because in far closer touch with their domestic and industrial life, than anything known to our experience. A single generation will see the exhaustion of our natural resources of oil and gas, and such a rise in the price of coal as will make the price of electrically transmitted water-power a controlling factor in transportation, in manufacturing, and in household lighting and heating. Our water-power alone, if fully developed and wisely used, is probably sufficient for our present transportation, industrial, municipal and domestic needs. Most of it is undeveloped, and is still in National or State control. To give away without conditions this, one of the greatest of our resources, would be an act of folly.
The question of state ownership, as regards hydro-electric energy, is one which might engage the attention of Parliament. I wish only to call to the attention of the members of the House the importance for Canada, as a quid pro quo, in case of a coal 'embargo, of public ownership of our water-

power system. The total possible horse power of Canada is estimated to be 18,203,000, and the developed horse power of Canada is only 1,813,200. I think the greatest national wealth of Canada to-day, bar none, is the watter-powers of the country. We have in Ontario and Quebec, and partially in the West, if properly harnessed and if controlled by the Government, an asset of inestimable value.
Now, another remedy which suggests itself for this fuel shortage is not only the exploitation of our peat bogs, the treatment of our lignites, the treatment and development of the shale rocks of Canada, and the development of our hydro-electric system, hut also the elimination of customs duties, war tax, etc., upon material and machinery needed for the exploitation and development of those different resources. Some time later in the session I will make a motion, just to test the views of the Government with regard to this question of tariff on material and machinery used for the development of our natural resources. It is a tentative motion; I placed it on the Order Paper last year, but it came to grief.
During the present session I intend to make the following motion:
That it is the opinion of the House that His Majesty's Government should make provision to prevent any recurrence of the late threatened scarcity of fuel.
That the present import duties and war tax, levied upon the material and machinery required for the construction of new hydroelectric power development, and for the desired electrical equipment of certain of Canada's steam railroads, also for the construction and equipment of works to produce peat fuel, fuel from lignite and to recover the oil contents of certain Canadian deposits of shale carrying oil, prevents the construction of such much to be desired plants and works.
That it is desirable that such power plants and fuel producing works should be developed and constructed, without further loss of time, and that to secure and encourage such development and construction, it is hereby resolved that during the continuance of the present war in Europe the import duties and war tax, now levied upon such material and machinery as are required for the development and construction of said power plants and fuel producing works shall no longer be so levied.
Here are, in a few words, the suggestions I have to offer the Government on this question of fuel shortage. It is
10 p.m. a very serious question for Canada and we shall have to face it very soon .as the spring .and summer will pass away in less time than we imagine. We shall be confronted next winter with a situation which might well appal the people of Canada. We know how certain homes suffered last winter. In the city of Ottawa, the capital of the Dominion, there

was misery, and if it had not been for the City Council of Ottawa and its worthy Mayor we would have had people actually freezing in many a home. The winter will soon be upon us, because we have practically no spring in Canada. We are actually at the opening of' summer, but we know it is of short duration. Winter will come and I beseech the Government that this is a proper time to study this question and to solve it, if it is possible of solution. The Government have appointed a Scientific Research Commission composed of some of the most distinguished scientists of 'Canada. I know Professor Macallum, a man who is imbued with the idea of service to his country. I hope that the 'Government will give Professor Macallum and his colleagues of the Scientific Research Commission the widest scope possible, in order to experiment and find a solution to the very serious problem I have placed before the House this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended' to say anything on this motion, reserving any remarks that I intended to make for the motion on the Order Paper standing in the name of the hon. member for East Lambton (Air. Armstrong). But there is a possibility that his motion may not be reached for some time, and I think, in justice to the people of Canada, especially those in the lower provinces, for whom I speak at the present moment, it is time that the Government take upon themselves seriously the matter of the fuel controller. The fuel controller is a joke, and we might as well face it. Last fall we had a visit from the fuel controller in our section. I may say frankly that owing to his visit to the Maritime Provinces, in the city of St. John alone we started in the month of November and continued throughout the very severe winter 15,000 tons of coal short. Why? Because, the fuel controller said that he was going to reduce prices, and he scared the people from buying coal. The result was that the coal remained in the bins of the coal merchants. They did not have room to put any more in; they could not import any, and we found ourselves this spring without the coal that normally would have been in the bins of the householders. Now, in January I took the trouble to take this matter up in. Washington with Air. Magrath. I pointed out to him the difficulties that we were going to face in the Maritime Provinces for coal in the coming winter of 1918-19. He informed me that we would have to burn soft coal in the lower provinces this coming winter, and that it would be just as well to go home and tell our people to change their grates so that they could burn soft coal. I thought that was rather strange, so next morning I took the trouble to go down and see Dr. Nasmith, the Chief of Staff of the United States Fuel Administration, and I was informed that on and after the first day of April coal would (be permitted to be ex-

ported from the United States, particularly anthracite coal, in the same proportion that it had moved for an average of three years previous to, the war. I immediately acquainted our coal authorises in the lower provinces with that fact, and they got busy to secure their coal supply. What did we find not later than last Friday? That the fuel controller in this country has made absolutely no arrangements for Canadian schooners in the port of New York, waiting for coal, to get their cargo. He should have made that arrangement with the United States Shipping Board, and now is not the time to consider it. He had fair warning two months ago. The result is that at present we have no coal in St. John, and there is very little in the province. This is the time of year when, as a rule, we begin to put in our anthracite coal for the following winter. For some reason or another, the fuel controller is playing into the hands of the big interests in Nova Scotia who produce coal. If we are to have a fuel controller, let him be a fuel controller. I listened with much interest to what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Meighen) said about the wonderful machinery that has been laid out for the fuel controller. ' That machinery was in operation last June.

Absolutely, that machinery was in operation last June. I could point to two or three men who were appointed by the fuel controller in the different provinces to act as his deputies. It is the same machinery exactly. I repeat that the fuel controller should be a fuel controller. Why was it that last year we in the lower provinces had to wait for bituminous coal while the Canadian Government railways imported the coal in their own steamers and handed it over to the Canadian Pacific rather than put the Canadian Pacific to the expense of taking it out of their bunkers? Why was it that last winter, when we needed coal that was consigned to our dealers in the lower provinces, simply because the Canadian Government railways did not have bunkers to put it in, they took the coal from the cars, and our people went without it? That is not fuel control; I think we ought to have a real fuel controller. It was reported some time ago that our Mr. Magrath was to resign, and the view was expressed that he should stay on. We should have .a fuel controller, and if Mr. Magrath is not the man to do this work, the appointment of another man to 
take his place should be seriously considered.
Union Government.

I have in my possession a statement over the signature of as reliable a man in the Maritime Provinces as you would want to know, that instructions have been issued by the fuel controller that coal may be moved to Ontario points, but not to lower province points.
I have not at hand a good deal of what I had intended to say this evening, and it will be necessary for me to curtail my remarks. I did not feel, however, that I could allow this motion to go by without calling the attention of the Government and of the House to the seriousness of this situation. It will not do to say that this matter will be taken up in April, in May, or in June; it will be too late then. Our production of bituminous coal must be looked after. If we cannot get the labour in this country to get the coal out, we will have to import the labour. I understand that the matter has been before Council; certainly it has not come before the House since I have been here. But we have to face the situation; unless we get bituminous coal, and get it quickly; unless we get production under way, half our industries will be closed next year. It is a well known fact that the fuel controller is a member of the War Trade Board; it would be interesting for Council to know how often he has attended the meetings of that body, with which he is supposed to co-operate. I have it on good authority that he has hardly attended a meeting of the War Trade Board, under the jurisdiction of which all these matters are supposed to come. I hope that the Government will not consider these remarks of mine as, a criticism of the Administration.

I have listened with interest to the discussion on .this question and in particular to the excellent .address delivered by the mover of the resolution. While I agree with many matters that have been brought up, I can-

not agree with the remarks made .by the bon. member for St. John ((Mr. Elkin) when he said that the fuel controller of this Government was a joke, because I believe, if this Govemmemt has in its employ or under its jurisdiction a man who is worthy of tlhe confidence of the Government and of the people of the Dominion of Canada, and .a man who is held in high respect and esteem by all classes of the people apart from their political affiliations, it is Mr. C. A. Magrath, fuel controller of the Dominion. I have known Mr. Magraltih for many years, .and it is very unfair that any lion, member, should make an attack on him personally when he has not the privilege of occupying a seat on the floor of this House, and is, therefore, unable to defend himself. For Mr. Magrath I hold no brief, but I speak of him only as I have personally found him, from my knowledge of his long connection with western life in Canada and the great service which .he has rendered in the development of that country. He is a gentleman who has been successful in his own private life and in. the public positions which he has. occupied in this country, and he has rendered valuable services to this Dominion in connection with the international waterways and as fuel controller, the position he now occupies. The criticisms are not fair, because, if you examine them, you will find they are based on, the simple fact that the Dominion Government has not had schooners in New York in order to take anthracite coal to St. John so that the people of that city may store it this spring, and then sit down and enjoy the heat next winter. The advice given by Mr. Magrath to my hon. friend was good, sound advice. Mr. Magrath, told him: You had better go home and tell your people to fit their grates up for bituminous coal. Is that not sound advices? Are they not in the centre of a district which produces more bituminous coal than any other district in the Dominion? Have they not the coal fields of Pictou, Inverness, Victoria, Cape Breton and Cumberland to draw upon? Can they not go there at any time during the summer and can they not go to .some of those ports, even in the winter and load their schooners with bituminous coal and take it to 'St. John, to keep the people in that city warm? If he was told by the director of fuel in the United States that there weuld (be 2,500,000 tons of anthracite coal coming to this country, and if he was told by Mr. Magrath that none of that would Ibe distributed in the Maritime Provinces, I feel that Mr. Magrath would be doing his duty, and this

Government would be doing their duty if they restricted the importation of that coal to the province of Ontario and that portion of the Dominion which lies west, including Manitoba and part of Saskatchewan. My hon. friend must realize that in Ontario we have no watercourses except some lakes, that in Manitoba and Saskatchewan we have no watercourses by which we can bring this anthracite coal from Pennsylvania. He must realize that one of the most serious problems we have had in the West in connection with the coal situation has been railway transportation, coupled with the labour problems which have been referred to by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). Does my hon. friend think that Mr. Magrath is going to give the people of the Maritime Provinces all that portion of the anthracite coal which they would 'like to have, because they have base-burners and .because anthracite coal is cleaner to handle, and, perhaps, gives out more heat? He must realize that we have passed through a very strenuous period during the past winter when hundreds of ocean-going boats were held up in Atlantic ports because of fuel shortage. He must realize that difficulty arose in regard to transportation over which the fuel controller of this country had no jurisdiction or control. He must realize that every part of this country has suffered from want of co al. He must realize that manufacturing industries have doubled their output during the past year; that they have been working night and day, and that it is more essential to this country that those factories he kept working than that people in New Brunswick and the Maritime Provinces be allowed to get in their usual supply of anthracite coal in order that they may live a little more luxuriously.	.

J d-o not represent a part of the country that is suffering from fuel shortage; in our part of the country we have all we require and are able to supply a good portion of western Canada. But I would like to offer a suggestion to the Government, and it relates somewhat to the question of anthracite coal mentioned by my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie). The mirlSs of western Canada unquestionably could supply the demands of western Canada, if the transportation facilities were available, and if we could always be sure of the conditions of the labour market. Given those conditions, all the anthracite coal at present going into Manitoba and parts of Saskatchewan could go to Ontario, for instance, where the shortage is the
greatest. But it is necessary first of all to make sure of the transportation facilities in order to get coal from the mines of Alberta east to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It is also important that the labour market should be assured all the year round. The chief difficulty with the mines of western Canada at present is that they are not sure of an all-the-year-round market, month in and month out, and until that is remedied it will be impossible to have a steady supply of labour, because miners are dissatisfied if they can secure only four or five months' work with one mine owner, and during the rest of the year have to look around for employment at other occupations. If we could arrange to provide the mines of western Canada with the entire western Canada market, it would assist to a great extent in meeting the labour situation. Of course, there has been the difficulty that western Canada coal has lost some of its fuel value when in storage, and dealers have not been anxious to store it foT that reason, but discoveries have been .made that seem to promise success, and I would suggest to the Government that they inquire into these proposed storage remedies either through the Conservation Commission or through the Fuel 'Controller s Department. Once the storage difficulty is overcome it will be possible for the dealers throughout the prairie provinces to acquire coal during the summer months for use in the fall and winter, and when we can do that, we can keep the mines in operation the year round, ^nd that will solve the labour difficulty. We have only tapped the coal resources
o.f western Canada. The mines of western Canada at the present time have a greater capacity than the demand of that country, and there are unlimited areas of coal as yet untouched. If the difficulties I have mentioned could be overcome, western Canada could supply the demands of all Ontario, I believe. Of course, Ontario is accustomed to using a hard coal, and we are accustomed to using a coal that is called soft, but it suits our purpose in every respect, and I am sure Ontario would find it quite useful, especially to meet shortages of the kind that occurred during last winter.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. H. BUTTS (South Cape Breton):
speechtext:
It would be inadvisable for a Cape Breton man to hold his tongue when the coal question comes up in such a manner as it has to-night. I wish to review the observations made by the mover of the resolution (Mr. COMMONS
Lemieux) and by my hon. friend from -North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and the very first suggestion I would like to make to them would be that, as far as the coal areas of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia are concerned, they might bring a little bit of influence to bear upon their friend the Premier of Nova Scotia to see if he would not really do something tangible to right the wrongs perpetrated by the local legislature of that province during the past twenty years. In Cape Breton County alone there are areas containing hundreds of millions of tons of coal that cannot be touched, belonging to the Dominion Coal Company, held under long leases and unworked. There are also other vast areas that cannot (be operated, (because the Dominion Coal Company properties are interlocked with those of the Nova Scotia Steel Company, and vice versa. Would it not be better for my two hon. friends, instead of making suggestions to the Government, to go to their friends in the Nova Scotia government and see if something could not be done to break the deadlock between those two companies? Not only are the towns suffering for coal, but the annual production of coal is actually decreasing year by year at the rate of some half a million tons yearly, and this notwithstanding the fact that great improvements have been made in mining machinery and production methods. The mover of the resolution came out with scare headlines about the shortage of coal.
In Central Canada.
Since Union Government?

I am speaking of Murray's Anti-Union Government of the last six years. Did it ever occur to them that the Port Hood mine was closed down, and that for about a week in that local House we fought for an investigation of the conditions prevailing at Port Hood? Did it ever occur to them that we had in Nova Scotia this last year two of the most terrible mining disasters that ever occurred in this country, which were only lost sight of on account of the overshadowing magnitude of the Halifax disaster? Did it ever occur to them to ask this House why it was that those disasters occurred? My hon. colleague and I can tell them that the accidents were due to the terrible mining laws and poor mining inspection existing in Nova Scotia. There was no more inspection of mines there than there is in the City of Quebec. Did it ever occur to those gentlemen that it would be well to look to their own household before they began to criticize others? A mine was closed down in the county of Pictou, at Thor-burn, not long ago, and no one has been told why. Another mine in West-ville was closed down and nobody has been told why.	This very high vein
of coal that my hon. friend from Cape Breton speaks of was not only 36 feet high, but it was 48, 50 and 60 feet, and it was closed down on account of bad mining laws and ineffective government inspection in Nova Scotia, and between 400 and 500 miners left the district. These are some of the matters that I suggest hon. gentlemen should think of before they begin to talk of the necessity of this Federal Government looking after the increased production of coal, which is primarily a provincial government matter. The increased production of coal in the eastern part of Canada is dependent upon the local government, and it is very greatly hampered by the local government, and I would say to these gentlemen that, at least for the sake of propriety, they had
better withdraw this resolution and look to their own household. They had better go to Mr. Murray and Mr. Armstrong, and the worthy Attorney General, Mr. Daniels, in Nova Scotia, and ask them if they cannot do their share to relieve the coal situation.

speechtext: Mr. J. E. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 31, to amend the Railway Act.
Explain.

This Bill is similar to the Bill I introduced in 1915. The legislation is along the same line as that which I have asked the Parliament of Canada, during the last five years, to hjing into force. It is for the purpose of bringing the boats engaged on our inland waters and our coastwise trade under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The railways in Canada are compelled to file their tolls, rates and tariff agreements with the Railway Board, and they are also compelled to do this with regard to boats connected with the railways.
I firmly believe it would be in the public interest not only to 'compel the boats on our inland waters and along the coast to file their tariff rates with the Board, but to bring them under the Board's absolute control. There are on the Canadian register 8,500 boats, with some 45,000 employees. In view of the fact that these boats are allowed to make use of our rivers, harbours, docks and cam-ate free of Charge, in which improvements the people o.f this country have invested over $350,000,000, I think horn, gentlemen will readily agree that it would be in the public interest for the Parliament of Canada to have control over these

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Sir George Foster, Minister of Trade and Commerce, the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolutions, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide for a Bureau under the Minister of Trade and Commerce to be called the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, to collect, abstract, compile and publish statistical information relative to the commercial, industrial, social, economic and general activities and condition of the people, to collaborate with all other departments of the Government in the compilation and1 publication of statistical records of administration, according to the regulations, and to take the census of the Dominion; and that the Governor in Council may appoint an officer to be called the Dominion Statistician to supervise and control the said Bureau; and that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, pay out of the moneys to be provided by Parliament for such purposes, such sums as are required for the taking of the census, collection of statistics, the remuneration of the officers and1 clerks, and the payment of all expenses incurred in carrying1 into effect an Act for such purposes.
We cannot hear a word of what is being said.
Come back and take your old seat, and you can hear.

Before the resolution is adopted, I should like to know from the minister what the purpose of the establish-
22 -
ment of this Bureau is. A lot of enumerations are contained in the resolution. There is one item which states that in this Bureau the statistics for the census will be taken. I thought there was a branch in the Department of Agriculture charged with the duty of collecting statistics regarding the census of Canada. Every now and then we receive a leaflet purporting to be statistics covered by this particular branch of the Department of Agriculture. This resolution also provides for the compilation and publication of statistical information relative to the commercial, industrial, social, economic and general activities and condition of the people. With reference to the first item, I thought the minister had a bureau or branch in his department, the special purpose of which was to collect statistics of commercial data. I know that we receive from time to time very interesting reports from the Department of Trade and Commerce, explaining the conditions of trade in various countries where the minister has representatives, who seem to report assiduously, and this information is conveyed to the people of Canada through those leaflets which were received monthly or bimonthly, I could not tell you which. I was under the impression, as far as the industrial statistics are concerned, that the Department of Labour had statisticians, whose duty it was to collect all these statistics relating to the industrial condition of the country, to the condition of the labouring classes, to the amount of work that is being performed, and the prices of various commodities, etc. Is the object of the minister to have in his department, and under his control, a Bureau of Statistics wherein all statistics which are now being gathered by the other departments, or by the various branches which are under the control of the other departments, would be collected, and is it the intention to have the whole thing merged into this department, and have a Bureau of Statistics wherein statistics of all kinds, whether relating to our foreign trade, or to our industrial, social, or general activities, would be collected? Perhaps it will not be necessary to deal with our social conditions, because the social columns of our newspapers will supply anybody who wants information along that line.
It might be a little different.

It might be, but I do not know that I would support the Minister of Trade and Commerce with reference to that particular branch of the statistical bureau.



I want to know whether all the other static tical branches in the various departments will he abolished or merged into this one great statistical department where information can toe had as to any branch of the service, or any statistics with reference to the condition of the country.

The thing is not as formidable as it appears at first blush and on reading it on the Order Paper. It was a matter of douibt really as to whether it would be necessary to put a resolution on the Order Paper or not as a foundation for the Bill, tout as that was the course that was pursued when the present Act was introduced, it was thought better to follow the rule on this occasion. Consequently, the resolution was placed on the Order Paper to form the foundation for the introduction of a Bill. My hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) was right in most of the impressions he had with reference to what is being done, tout he was a little bit out in the allocation of the services which _ he enumerated to the different departments. What it is meant to do is to consolidate, and make some few amendments to, the law as it is at present upon the statute book and as it is administered in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The object of the consolidation and ratification of the legislation which is at present on the statute books to make the law more effective. It is designed, as it is provided now under the law, that there shall toe a central statistical board or office. It is proposed to call that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics as being a somewhat more apposite name for the work which is toeing carried on and as being in line with the nomenclature in other countries. The idea underlying the present law, and which will underlie these amendments, is that general economic statistics shall toe under the supervision of, and be issued by, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The different departments will, of course, Tetain their administrative, or record, statistics, or such statistics as are necessary for the administration of the department. There will be no change in that respect. Then, again, during the last three years-not to make the story long, 'because I propose to go a little more fully into it when I introduce the Bill,-a great deal has been done to coordinate the work in connection with the Dominion statistics tooth in the gathering, compilation and distribution, with the different provincial statistical departments. By conference and good will, an understanding has been reached with all of these along 
certain lines, the idea being to do away with overlapping and to have a uniform basis upon which the information is gathered so that the statistics will have a comparative value and so that there will be no contradiction between them. We have suffered a great deal with respect to the prestige of our statistics by having different computations put forward toy different provinces and by the Dominion almost always arising from the fact that there has never been a uniform basis1 upon which the questions have been issued, on the answers to which the information is compiled. On the introduction of the Bill I shall ask the House to listen a little more at length to an exposition of the measure.

I would assume that in preparing the Bill and talking the matter over with the officials the details bad been very carefully considered. Will this relieve any of the other departments from any work now undertaken toy their statistical branches, or will it leave the other departments, and their statistical branches, in, the same position as they now occupy and with the same work as they now do?

My hon. friend
will see that the resolution provides for the co-operation of the central statistical bureau with the departments and if it is found, as it has already be-eir found-and in some cases it is in operation-that the two can work in co-operation with each other and reach .a better result, that co-operation will take place. Provision is made for co-working between the different departments and the central statistical Bureau. The object is to confine the departments to record or administrative statistics ,and leave the field of general economic statistics to the central bureau.
Is there any provision for collecting data on labour?

Yes, to a certain extent. Any central system of statistics must take in capital and wages, labour employed and so on; but the special statistics of labour are under the Labour Department and will remain untouched.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why not under the same head?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I thought I heard my right hon. friend a .moment ago, when we were in committee, declare that it was his intention to explain the Bill at some length.

When I move for the second reading.

speakerposition: topic
