speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Reid (Minister of Railways), the House again went into committee on Bill No. 14, to confirm an agreement between His Majesty the King and the Van Buren Bridge Company, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On the schedule.

Mr. Chairman, 1 had
a,n interview with the Miiuiister of Railways yesterday afternoon with reference to this Bill. He informed me that he was going to see the Bill through, and that I could put before the House all 'the objections possible; but he was bound to see it through. From hois remarks when this Bill was last before the committee I noticed that the [DOT]minister did not understand everything in reference to this matter. He .stated to me that we would have an interview and that, no . douibt, the matter would come out all right. As a minister of the Crown, the hon. gentleman seems to :me to be fair. minded, but I am sorry to say that he is a stubborn gentleman; and I am afraid that 'he feels himself obliged to see this Bill through the House. I am very sorry for the public that the Minister of Railways has taken this step, for, after all, we are here to protect the public interest, and the Minister of Railways should 'be the first man to set a good example.
I know the locality where it is proposed to change the site of the union station. The proposed station is altogether outside the town of St. Leonards, a distance of between a quarter and half a mile. We have had petitions and telegrams of protest read to the House. I have also received lettens from business men, and notwithstanding all these protests coming from the whole corporation of the town of St. Leonards, my hon. friend is still under the impression that this union station should be built on the Transcontinental railway. I had from the Minister of Railways yesterday
22i
afternoon promises that the welfare of the public will be looked after.
At the present time, the Transcontinental railway has one train going east and one train going west daily. The train going east passes through the town of St. Leonards at twelve o'clock midnight. The train going west passes through at three o'clock in the morning. The Intercolonial railway train arrives at St. Leonards at three o'clock in the afternoon. The Canadian Pacific railway runs an express reaching St. Leonards at five o'clock in the afternoon, accommodating the public by running a train during the day. Now, if the location of the station is changed, I am sorry to say that the public will be forced to travel from the union station on the Transcontinental railway about half a mile to take the train at the Canadian Pacific railway station, You will not stop the public from travelling over the Canadian Paoific railway.
The day before yesterday I Tead a telegram in the Hous^in reference to the protest of the people of St. Leonards regarding this Bill. I also stated in the House that the people of St. Leonards were strongly against the proposal contained in this Bill unless the terminus of the Intercolonial railway should remain where it is at present. The ex-Minister of Railways, Hon. Mr. Cochrane, promised the people of St. Leonards^ that no change should he made, and I am sorry to see that the present Minister of Railways does not see eye to eye with his predecessor. I, therefore, Mr. Chairman, protest most energetically against the passing of this Bill, and I want to request the Minister of Railways, if he will be kind enough to listen to me, that [DOT]before he commences to move that station from the International railway to the National Transcontinental railway, he come himself to the town of St. Leonards and visit the site where he proposes to build the new station. I am sure of one thing from the good judgment of my hon. friend, that after seeing the proposed site, he will in common with the residents of St. Leonards, be opposed to the site of the new station.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

There is a great deal
of territory that my hon. friend has not yet covered as Minister of Railways, and this is a part of the country where he has not the least idea of local conditions. Before passing this Act, or before moving the present station from the International railway .to the Transcontinental railway, I would ask the minister to come when the

session is over and see for himself and thereby convince himself that he is wrong and that I am right.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this Bill was before the committee a few evenings ago, my hon. friend Stated that he understood that the charter given by this House for this piece of railway had a clause in it that the station would not be moved from where it is at the present time. The hon. member (Mr. Michaud) and I have discussed that point, and we have found the objection was not well founded. The situation as it has been laid before us by the officials of the Government railway system is this: the Government operates the Transcontinental railway between Levis and Moncton, which runs through the town of St. Leonards and has a station there. After the Transcontinental railway had been completed the Government purchased what is known as the International railway, running from a point on the Intercolonial line to St. Leonards, a distance of one hundred and twelve miles. The International railway had been in operation for some years and had its own terminal station. Since the purchase of that line the Government has had to maintain two stations in the town of St. Leonards, although it is the owner of both railways. But there was no connection between the International and the Transcontinental railway systems. Therefore, the traffic going over the International line, intended for the Transcontinental, has to be taken over this two miles of railway that we are leasing, and for which we have to pay the owners of the stretch in question, namely, the Bangor and Aroostook Company. The management of the Government railways discussed the matter with me, and we came to the conclusion that a connection should be made between the two railway systems. Negotiations were entered into, with the result that we are leasing the stretch of two miles, as has been shown in the agreement attached to the Bill. The objection raised by the hon. member (Mr. Michaud) is that if we carry out this agreement the Government, as the owner of both railways, will only use one station, that of St. Leonards, .and the International railway will run its trains into the station maintained for the Transcontinental. It must either do that, or else continue running to the station of the International railway. It would be impossible to use the latter station because the Transcontinental could not go around and over to it. Therefore,

as a matter of business, and in the interest of the country, it does not seem reasonable to my mind that we should continue to run the International trains over the two miles in .question to that station, and at the same time .maintain the statioft that has been used by the International railway. The hon. member states that if we do away with the station, as proposed, *people wishing to travel on the Canadian Pacific railway will have to go from the Transcontinental Railway station to that of the Canadian Pacific railway. If I understand the situation, and my facts have been gathered .from our officials, the International station as it now exists and the Canadian Pacific Railway station are very close together, and there is very little distance between them. The Transcontinental Railway station, from the information I have, is not far away, and at most passengers will have to travel but a few hundred feet. Why should the Government operate the International railway and keep up 4 p.m. that station in order that people may have to walk a few hundred feet less to travel on the Canadian Pacific railway? On the other hand, people travelling by the International railway who wish to take the Transcontinental railway have to walk a longer distance to reach the latter railway. The object in leasing this small *piece of line is, as I have stated: First, it is, in my opinion, an absolute necessity that we have a connection between the two railways in order to permit of the carriage of freight on our railways over the Transcontinental. Either we had to build two miles of line or else lease the needed section as we have done. Furthermore, in order to effect economy and save useless expenditure it is intended to only have one station for the two railways. The hon. member (Mr. Michaud) states that if I were to visit that portion o.f the country I would see the necessity of continuing the station which it is proposed to close. All I can say to my hon. friend is that I have gone into this matter very carefully. I believe it is in the interest of the public, and of the great railway systems concerned, that this connection should be made .between the International and the Transcontinental railway. In my opinion, the connection proposed here is the cheapest and best that could be made. Even if we were to build the two miles stretch instead of leasing it, it would still, in my opinion, only be necessary to have the one station. If this Bill passes we will secure the needed' connection and it will be of great advantage for freight

traffic, at all events. As far as making the one .station seryie for the two railway systems, that policy is correct, from the information in. imy possession, and I cannot hold out to the hon. gentleman 'any prospect of letting the two stations remain. When the opportunity of passing through that district is afforded me, if any evidence should toe presented that would justify the retention of the two stations, it will toe taken into consideration. In. the meantime, we are exceedingly anxious to have this connection at the earliest possible moment, even for freight traffic, and I hope the hon. gentleman will not further object to assisting us in facilitating the passage of the Bill for the reasons that I have mentioned.

I am sorry to say that I cannot assist the hon. gentleman in passing this Bill. Local public sentiment is opposed to it, as evidenced by the long adverse petition presented toy the citizens of St. Leonards. I know the conditions in that locality, and in view of all the circumstances,, I cannot concur in the minister's decision to close up the station in question. The minister has stated that the question involved is one of business for the Transcontinental railway. In my opinion, it is a matter of business for the people of that part of New Brunswick. When he states that there are only a few hundred feet to be covered between the two stations, I would like to say it is a distance of a quarter or half a mile.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: About thirteen hundred feet.

At all events, we will
let the question of the distance stand for the /moment. I would ask the minister if he will 'be kind enough not to make any change with respect to the proposed union station until he makes his trip through that part of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I could not make that promise. The sittings of the House may 'detain me here too long.

I am not sufficiently acquainted with the local conditions to be able to say whether the minister is consulting the public convenience in locating the union station at the place referred, to. I would ask, however, if the making of this *agreement involves the dismantling and tearing up of two miles of the International railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

And is he also closing the
station on the International railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is the intention.

I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that he is doing away with a section of railway which was purchased not very long ago. I do not recollect the price per mile paid for this railway, but at all events he is dismantling and doing away with a section of two miles. From a business standpoint he is simply throwing away two miles of this railway, tearing up the rails and dismantling this portion of the road. While doing this, he is leasing from the Bangor and Aroostook railway two miles of railway alt the annual rental of $1,200. So far as the business life of a railway company is concerned, it is only a short time between now and 1934, and at the end of that period, during which you have thrown away these two miles of railway which you have bought and paid for, and have inconvenienced the people of that locality, taking away from them the railway privileges which they have had for years, and during which period you have paid an annual rental of $1,200. Whoever happens to be occupying the position of Minister of Railways at that time will be up against the proposition that he has to retrace his steps and rebuild the two miles of railway, or purchase these two miles of railway that the Government had under lease, or else enter into a new lease. I am speaking only from a business standpoint; I am not speaking from the standpoint of convenience to the citizens of that locality, because 1 do not know the circumstances, and I am taking my information only from what my hon. friend (Mr. Michaud) has told this committee. I would like to ask the minister what it costs per year to keep the International Railway station open, what help is employed there, and what it would cost per year to keep the station in existence.
There is only one employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Perhaps I can answer the two questions at once. The hon. member states that this Government are going to be out $1,200 per annum from now until 1P34, that being the rental mentioned in the lease, and that we shall have nothing to offset that. The hon. member knows that, when we take up two miles of rails, those rails are worth at the present time probably $17,000 or $18,000, and if that money were invested in Dominion Government bonds, it would bring in interest sufficient to pay the $1,200 per annum, so that there is really no pecuniary loss. I cannot say offhand how many officials are at that

station, but I know there is an agent, and he probably receives $600 or $700 a year, so that we are saving at least that amount. The hon. member also states that the people of that locality are being deprived of their railway facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not know it' either,
but the plan that has been submitted to the House will show it. People coming in to or leaving St. Leonard on the International leave at a certain station of the International that has1 been there for a number of years. The Transcontinental is a few hundred feet to the south of the International, which means that if you want to take a train on the International, you go a few hundred feet further from whatever part of the town you live in. There is no inconvenience further than that, and so far as the Government are concerned, we shall have this advantage, that if we were to take up the rails and dispose of them, the interest on the amount received for the rails would cover the amount we have to pay as rental, and we shall save the amount which we have been, paying for our cars going over that road during the whole of the year, cars being transferred from the International to the Transcontinental, and which must amount to a considerable sum of money. We shall also save the salaries of the employees who are kept at the station and of those who are engaged in maintaining the tv o miles of railway. I cannot understand where there would be much inconvenience, except that any passengers coming in on the International, who wanted to go on the Canadian Pacific might, so far as I can judge from the map, have to walk probably two or three hundred feet from the International to the Canadian Pacific, whereas, if they wanted to go on the Transcontinental, they might have to walk ten or twelve hundred feet.
The passengers would not have to walk any distance at all because the International train runs into the Canadian Pacific station.

In answering my question the minister opened up a new phase of the matter, pointing out that the Government would not lose anything; that, as a matter of fact, there would be a financial gain to the Government to take up and dismantle these

two miles of railway because, as the minister says, the rails could be sold at a high price owing to the present demand, and the interest on the money received, if invested in Victory Bonds, would more than pay the annual rent provided for in the lease between the Government and the Bangor and Aroostook railway. If one were to follow the minister'si argument along that line, one could take up the rails on any piece of railway and make money on the transaction. That, however, is not what, as I understand it, the Government intend doing. I understood from the minister that it was in the interest of the Transcontinental railway to enter into this agreement for the leasing of this road; that it was to do away with the keeping up of two stations. Now, he says, from a business standpoint, it is to the benefit of the Government to take up these rails and invest the money received for them, because the interest on that investment will more than cover the annual rental of $1,200. I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that at the end of 1934, when this lease expires, the Government will be called upon to enter into a new lease, or to buy the road, or to rebuild the two miles of railway that has been torn up, and if, during that period, $ie cost of rails increases, then the Government will be out a very large amount to rebuild, reestablish and re-equip the two miles of railway which they have in their possession and which they are throwing away rather than keep that road in operation. One of the reasons the minister gives for his action is that it will do away with the expense of keeping up the International Railway station. He says himself there was only one official there whose salary would be about $600 or $700. Yet he is paying to the Bangor and Aroostook railway $1,200 per annum for the purpose of doing away with a station on the International railway. From a business standpoint, my hon. friend from Restigouche (Mr. Michaud), in opposing this proposition, is making only a reasonable argument, and the minister has not made out a proper case so far as the financial advantage of the Government and the interest of the railway are concerned. The minister says that he knows nothing about the location and, of course, we accept his word in regard to the matter. If we did not accept his word from a Parliamentary standpoint, we would know, from the agree* merit he is making in regard to the matter, that he does not know anything about it, and that he is depending entirely upon some railway official in regard to it. The minister

will not be Minister of Railways very long before he will come to realize fully that frequently young engineers from some school who are taken into the service, will, during the summer months when they have nothing else to do, go over the Intercolonial and make faddy recommendations without regard to the interests of communities which have had railway accommodation for years.
My hon. friend must not forget that the usual thing is for a town or village to build up around a station, and the station become the very heart of the community. I think the minister, before taking away the station which these people have had for so many years, should give some better reason to the House, or he might let the matter stand for further consideration.

I should like to hear from the minister as to the policy of the Government in such a case as this. Around the station at Cape Traverse, for instance, there is a large vested interest, and before the Government do away with that station I think we should have a statement from the minister whether it is right and proper to deprive these people of their rights. I have no doubt that the officials who have recommended this union station at St. Leonard's are acting in the interests of the Government system, but is it honest or just to do away with the other station regardless of the rights of individuals? I think one of the principles embodied in British justice is that the individual stands above the community, and where an individual has to suffer rather than a corporation the individual's interest should at least be recognized.

The hon. member for Russell has asked me to explain what the programme of the Imperial Munitions Board has been, and how it affects the present programme of the Canadian Government. I reply by stating that when I had the honour of being called to the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries and Naval Service, I found that the Dominion Government was advancing money through the Imperial Munitions Board, under the direct management of Sir Joseph Flavelle, to keep all of the steel shipyards in Canada fully occupied in building ships for the Mother Country. It seemed to me, and also to the Government when I brought the matter to their attention, that the time was opportune for Canada to embark upon the building of steel ships as a national, permanent policy.

These are not days when the policy of protection needs be discussed, and as we are more concerned with the prosecution of the war than with tariff matters, I did not raise the tariff question with my colleagues at all, nor do I intend to do so with hon. members of this House. In 'brief, the contract that I have concluded with the Dominion Iron andi Steel Company of Sydney was made- on the following basis-: The Dominion Government have guaranteed to the .Dominion Iron and -Steel Company of -Sydney that they will have a -minimum tonnage of fifty thousand tons of ship plates a year, extending over a period of five years, making in -all a to-tal tonnage of two hundred and fifty thousand tons-. We have taken, as a basis to adjust this price every six months, the price per ton of steel ingots. The price at the time the contract was entered into for steel ingots was $25.50 per ton. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government,
and I, as the minister charged with the responsibility of seeing that the Government's shipbuilding programme is carried out, looked very carefully into that question, but, as I stated in my remarks a few minutes ago, the Government's policy being only to keep the steel shipbuilding yards in Canada busy, our financial ability will not permit us to go beyond that. My hon. friend from South Quebec (Mr. Power) will agree that, as a business proposition and as a national proposition, hearing in mind that these ships are being built not for to-

day only, tout for the future, it is a wiser policy for Canada to put her money into steel shipbuilding than to put it into wooden ships. I am not saying anything derogatory to the wooden ships, but the speed of a wooden ship is very much less than that of a steel ship, her carrying capacity is less, and the wooden ship is debarred from the submarine zone because her speed being so slow, she presents a very much better target for submarine torpedoes. But the latter argument is not the one that causes 'the Government to go in for steel shipbuilding. The other arguments which I have just presented carried more weight.

I suppose, in a
matter of such importance, with so many details, we should all feel disposed to reserve our judgment on matters of detail, so that if any question arises later on we may be free to inquire into it. Subject to that I want to offer my congratulations to the hon. 'Minister of Marine and Fisheries on the exceedingly interesting and most admirably clear statement he has made on an undertaking of so much importance to the country. I think the House has received the announcement very favourably, and we shall all desire, when the details come to be considered, that there may he nothing found in them which- will lead us to withdraw our good opinion of the minister's programme.
I think the Government should be congratulated upon giving their attention just now to steel shipbuilding which of course does not necessarily imply that they lack appreciation of the importance of wooden shipbuilding. My own judgment is that we do not need any particular stimulus for wooden shipbuilding in our country. It is an art with which many of our people are quite familiar. I do not know whether there is a revival in the ancient city of Quebec of the great art of wooden shipbuilding, hut in the Maritime Provinces there is a very large measure of activity all along our coast. In my own constituency several wooden ships are being built. I am afraid the conflict between iron and wood and steel was settled some years ago when, in the age of progress through which we were passing, the fact had to be recognized that the wooden ship must give way to the iron ship, and the iron ship in turn must give way to 'the steel ship. By and by we will return to those conditions when tlhe large wooden ships will hardly have much chance in competition with the large steel ships. There has been in the past, and I believe there will be in the future, quite

a demand for wooden ships of the smaller class. I believe the conditions thaJt will exist at the close of the war, and for some years after the war, will be such that there will be large opportunity for the wooden shipbuilders of the country to engage .in their enterprise. So that I feel that, in giving the preference to steel shipbuilding, as the hon. minister is doing, there is no danger of any injustice being done to the wooden shipbuilding industry. I believe that industry will flourish for some years to come without .any particular aid from the Government.
Steel shipbuilding is, in a measure, a new industry here. It has been carried on in a small way, but owing to the very fact that the hon. gentleman has stated: that we had no plate mill in the country, we could not expect to engage in the enterprise in a very large way. As I happen to know something of the formation of the Dominion Steel Company, and as I was, in some measure, identified in a modest degree some years ago with the creation of this splendid industry in 'Cape Breton, I take a particular pleasure to-day in hearing the minister make the announcement that he is arranging to. have a contract with the Dominion Steel Company, whereby the steel plates will be made in the works at Sydney. Altogether, I am sure the House has been deeply interested in the statement of my hon. friend, and I offer him my hearty congratulations on it.

In harmony with this acclaim of congratulations this afternoon, I wish to. congratulate the minister, but on somewhat different grounds. The .minister said he was able to induce people to start a valuable industry in this country by allowing their machinery to come in free, or rather allowing the machinery to come in on payment of the diuty -and afterwards refunding the duty to these people.

That was done in a
moment of weakness.

The point I wish to
make is that, if it is a good thing in Canada to permit manufacturers to bring in free of duty machinery for making ships,
it might be a good, thing in Canada to allow machinery for other purposes- to- be brought in free. I would not like this occasion to pass without saying that I hope that the minister's attitude that no large industry can be started or perpetuated in Canada without artificial encouragement by means of a bonus or tariff will not be endorsed. I would not like that statement to pass unchallenged, because I trust he is wrong. I trust there are industries in this- country which do not need any encouragement by bounty or tariff. The building of ships is a -war measure. If -artificial stimulation is required it should he given, but it should not be given-, I take it, as a matter of principle. My recollection, of course, does not go so far back as the- recollection of the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) but I am old enough to know that the industrial history of this country is emphasized here and there by large companies who enjoyed bounty encouragement and tariff encouragement, and who, when they were making too much profit, capitalized that profit against the people of Canada by watering their stock in most lavish fashion. I make these remarks not in any way to detract from the congratulations that have been showered on the minister-because he deserves these congratulations for the way he has placed this matter before the House-but in order to put myself, and, I believe, some of my friends on both sides of the House, on record that we are not absolutely wedded to the principle of protection.

I was going to remark, however, with regard to the great shipbuilding problem before this country at present, that I had the pleasure of visiting British Columbia recently, and while there went through one of the shipyards that the ihon. minister stated he has given a contract to, the Wallace Shipbuilding Company at Vancouver. I am rather surprised that none of the members from British Columbia' have spoken on this question, because I saw there the most marvellous development of shipbuilding that -can, possibly be found in the world. I stood in that shipyard and saw the workmen moulding the plates for the building of the ships. One of the most intricate pieces of work in connection with shipbuilding is the making of the bilge plates of a beautiful steel ship. Four men were handling that plate. Not a blow was being struck, not a bit of human muscle was being exercised, no brawn was being used except in simply moving the plate along to receive the pressure that was coming from the mountain that stood within view of the very men that were handling the plate. There they weTe, drawing energy from " white coal " which was generated from a mountain lake, and they were moulding that plate into that intricate shape, ready to put on the ship's bottom, without using a mallet, a chisel, or a maul. It was a marvellous thing, and it showed that the people of British Columbia, at any rate, have all the necessary elements to compete with anything in the world in the building of ships. I found that not only were they moulding plates by means of electrical energy, but they were cutting off their great beams with an instrument just like a pencil following a line, cutting off great beams, six inches square, with a jet of electric flame, and the celebrated acetylene gas that is used in connection with it. All the riveting and that sort of thing is being done by the same power. There is no doubt in the world but that we can build ships in Canada. We built them before. There was a time in our history, in the early sixties, I think, when



Canada-little undeveloped Canada-stood second, or, at any rate, third, in the whole coterie of the nations of the earth in point of tonnage. And, during those years the men who went down to the sea in ships from the Maritime Provinces and the province of Quebec were second to no men in the world. They were first. Very few sailors amongst them, because they were not very long at the business, but they developed to such a marvellous extent into officers that one would think they were all precocious boys. I have seen young men, taken out of the green woods in the province of Prince Edward Island, in two years' time become masters of square rigged ships in the foreign service; they were the greatest successes that any country ever produced. Anything that the hon. minister can do to build up a mercantile navy I am sure will be to the interest of Canada as a whole, as well as to the interest of those centres which have the good fortune to have the industry established amongst them.
I want it to be distinctly understood that I do not endorse any of that stuff that I read from the Halifax Herald.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In answer to the hon. gentleman, it has not come to my notice that we have had any difficulty at all in placing orders for steel ships in Canada. Whenever the berths become vacant we find the shipbuilders eager and anxious for business. It has1 not been brought to my [DOT] notice that there is any condition such as my hon. friend has mentioned.
Will the hon. minister inform the committee why there is such a large decrease in the item compared with last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will notice that the vote for this same item in 1917-18 amounted to $1,000,000. We are asking the House to vote now $600,000, which is $400,000-less than last year. I will give the reason for the reduction very briefly. This is a reduction of $400,000 on the esti-
mates passed for the fiscal year 1917-18. Last year the vote was partly nominal, as stores purchased and distributed to Canadian, British and Allied vessels in connection with the prosecution of the war were charged to this vote, and refunds were then credited thereto. For the present year the system of bookkeeping for store expenditures has been changed and such expenditures will be charged directly to the war vote, any refund's being credited to that vote. The item for the coming year is to cover the cost of maintaining the Royal Naval College, the expenditure on headquarters permanent naval staff and some of the expenditures of the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt. I might explain that it is the policy now for Canada to be called upon by the Imperial Government to furnish provisions for a great many of the Imperial ships at Halifax and at Esquimalt. Canada supplies the provisions necessary for these British ships and we charge the amount to the Imperial Government, and it is refunded later. Charging a certain sum this year to the war appropriation is the reason the amount is $400,000 less than last year.

I would like to get from the minister some information as to this vote. How many wireless stations are under the control of the department? How many .men are employed? Is the department encouraging the study of radiotelegraphy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have at the present time 184 coast, land and ship stations in Canada, of which 66 are Govern-

ment land and ship stations. The total personnel employed in the Dominion is 506, 239 of whom are in the Government employ, and 276 are employed by commercial companies. We have a school in Ottawa with about sixty attending.

What are the arrangements for the students? Do they get scholarships? Is the Government paying them directly or indirectly to study radiotelegraphy? The minister will, of course, understand this is a very important item. Wireless telegraphy has rendered great service to the navy and to the merchant marine, and its use has become universal. I am quite sure that when peace is restored wireless telegraphy will be of immense service for our ships at sea. In normal times, we know, the S.O.S. call in the midst of the ocean has saved many ships. It will be interesting to know that the Department of Marine and Fisheries of Canada is encouraging the study of radiotelegraphy. I am pleased to be able to say that Canada .was the first country to encourage Signor Marconi to establish the system, the first official station being bonused by the Canadian Government. It is quite a credit to Canada, and I would be glad to know that, under the direction of the minister, similar encouragement will be given in the future. I understand that the department was represented some few years ago at a congress of radiotelegraphy held in Europe, I think at London, at which rules and regulations were drafted and accepted by a number of the governments of the world. Perhaps the minister is not familiar with the sittings of that congress, but he might, at some later date, give the House information on that subject. At all events, I wish to state that it would be a most interesting development for Canada and for the future of our merchant marine that wireless stations on board ships be 'made compulsory.	1

Later on, when the war is over, I would like the hon. minister to look into the matter of wireless telegraphy from the point of view of state ownership. Actually, we are paying very high rates for cablegrams. It is true that there has been a reduction in the rates of some cable companies, due to a long agitation, although that reduction has been withdrawn during the war, except at certain times. I think that every Saturday evening cablegrams can. be sent at reduced rates if addressed to some one in the army or connected with the military service. But after the war is over, the hon, minister, as head of the department supervising this service, should concentrate his attention on that phase of the question, namely a reduction in the tolls for transmitting telegrams across the
There has been in the British Empire during the last twenty-five years a constant agitation, first to reduce the postal rates and the cable rates. It has been, found, after practical experiment, that the lower the rates the more money came into the treasury. The apostles of that postal reduction were, first, Rowland Hill, -and 'later Mr. Henniker Heaton, the member 'for Canterbury, England. He was an Australian, by the way, but he sat in the British House of Commons for twenty-five years. He died at Geneva at the 'beginning of the war. But he agitated until finally he was the chief promoter of the postal conference which, under the Duke of Norfolk, brought about the two-eent rate throughout the British Empire; and it is well to remember that this reduction was proposed by the then
[Mr. Ballantvne.l
Postmaster General of Canada, Sir William Mulock. But the agitation didi not stop there. Mr. Heaton was engaged even up to the time of his death in an endeavour to secure a reduction in the cable rates; and, ae the cable companies were strongly opposed to any such reduction, Mr. Henniker Heaton, in league with SignoT Marconi, was about to obtain cheaper rates for the transmission of wireless communications.
It seems to me that Canada, being the largest and oldest Dominion in the Empire, is very much interested in this matter of cheaper communication by wireless with the Mother - Country. We are interested because we have such a large flow of immigration from the British Isles, and these immigrants, largely settlers in the West, are at times, because of their family connections on the other side, obliged to have rapid transmission of messages to their folks at home. We know that a letter takes too long to travel, although before the war we were blessed with a relatively fast steamer service across the Atlantic. Not only are we interested from the point of view of communications which may pass privately between our immigrants in the West and their families in the British Isles, but we are also largely interested in getting a cheap news service for our newspapers. The news which comes from Europe in ordinary times is more or less tainted- and I do not use that word in any offensive sense-with the American touch.
Hew about the North-cliffian touch?

I am not referring to individuals. But it seems to me of the utmost importance that we should get a cheap news service direct to Canada without relying on the service to New York, Boston or other points in the United States. I am speaking of conditions that would obtain in normal times if we ean establish a wireless system which will compete with the cable companies, and it is only by competition that we shall have cheaper rates.
Now, this is a very important point, in my judgment. Some years ago, when I had the honour to be Postmaster General of Canada, I obtained from the Postmaster General of England cheap postal rates for British newspapers and magazines, and as a result these were to be seen in every railway station and bookstore in Canada. I made a calculation at the time, and by comparing the dead weight of the number of bags and baskets at Rimouski and Hali-

fax filled with magazines and newspapers, found that in less than six months after having obtained that cheap postal rate we had nearly doubled the circulation of these periodicals, and after a year or so there was - no more comparison, because the country was flooded with them. I thought it was a good service to Canada that we should, at all events, give the preference to that literature. I am sorry to say that for the last three or four years the arrangement between the two post offices has not been renewed; and, whilst I do not wish to discuss postal matters on this item, I desire to impress upon my hon. friend that he should not lose sight of the fact that for cheap news from Britain to Canada he must rely on the wireless system, because that system will give the necessary competition to the private-owned cable companies, and competition will bring down the rate. That is the reason I asked this evening if there was a school attached to the department in order to promote the system of radiotelegraphy. I believe in the future of radiotelegraphy, and I think it will be a blessing for Canada when we have stations dotting our shores from the 45th parallel as far north as possible, and when we have direct communication by wireless, not only with the British Isles, but from our western coast, with Japan. I hope I have not transgressed the rules too much, and I hope my hon. friend will accept my views in a good spirit, and will give heed to some of the advice which I have given him free of charge.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the minister's attention to a matter concerning the ports on the south shore of Nova Scotia. Several of these ports, owing to the severe winter which we have passed through, have been closed or obstructed by ice. If I am not mistaken, and the horn, member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) will correct me if I am, the port of Lunenburg was thus obstructed. Lunenburg is the most important fishing port in the Dominion. The port of Shelburne was obstructed. It is one of the finest harbours we have in the country. The port of Yarmouth, the gateway of western Nova Scotia, with its important traffic, also suffered some obstruction. In all these cases application had to be made to the Department of Marine and Fisheries for relief, and I am glad to be able to say that in every case the minister and his staff did the best they could in the matter, and that some relief was granted The object of my present remarks is to suggest to my hon. friend that it would be very desirable, in view of difficulties of that character, if a vessel suitable for the purpose were assigned to that class of service for a short period during the winter, probably about a couple of months. It would not need a powerful icebreaker of the class needed in the St. Lawrence region, A vessel or boat ordinarily employed for other purposes, but perhaps equipped with some little extra sheathing or something of the sort, located, perhaps, at Halifax, ito be ready for service of that character, would be able to render very necessary and valuable service. The ice which forms in these ports is not very thick and if attended to promptly it could be disposed of easily if the proper appliances were available, whereas, if it is allowed to become solid, difficulty may arise. The people in that part of the country appreciate the efforts of the Department of Marine and Fisheries to give them relief and are grateful for what has been done, but I would suggest to the hon. gentleman for his consideration whether i't would not be well to assign a special vessel to spend a couple of months at Halifax and be ready for an emergency of that character.
IMr. BALLANTYNE: I will be very glad to see if that cannot be done for another season. I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has brought the matter to my attention.
Mr. LEM'IEUX: I wish to make the same request for the harbour of Gaspe. Gaspe is the greatest poTt of Canada. That is where the fleet assembled after the boys left Valcartier camp for England., You have probably 6een the picture of the fleet that anchored in the harbour of Gaspe when the boys left for the front. Every year-after the ice is clear in the gulf and after navigation has opened, the interesting population of Gaspe is bottled up. The farthest point of the bay is very narrow, the ice is very thick and the people are bottled up. There is no communication.
After several S.O.S. calls, during many years, the Marine Department decided to send, generally in April, one of the ice breakers or one of the other big steamers of the department to facilitate the opening of the harbour. The minister will probably hear from the people of Gaspe on the opening of navigation, and in making this request now I am simply giving him an advance notice.

The inauguration of the car ferry system on the Straits of Northumberland has done away with the necessity of maintaining the winter boats, I hope for all time to come, thanks in large measure to the Prime Minister.
*Let me say that the car ferry is -an unqualified success, and has performed a service that nobody expected to be so successful. The car ferry is a tremendous ice-breaker, probably one of the best in the world, and its operation has changed the conditions down there.
