Notwithstanding that fact, however, the congestion of freight in Prince Edward Island was never so abnor-

mal as it is to-day. Everything in the way of freight was held up very largely all the winter, mainly because of difficulties arising in connection with the railroads. I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that a large portion of our produce still awaits shipment to the mainland, and a great deal of it is of a perishable nature. When the spring comes this produce must be got across to the mainland or it will be lost altogether. At a time like the present we do not want such a loss of produce to the Dominion if it is at all possible to avoid it. The two ports of Sum-9 p.m. merside and Charlottetown have always been opened by the winter steamers in the .spring. This year I presume the Stanley will not be in juxtaposition to these ports, and, therefore, will not be able to open them up. I would, therefore, ask the head of the department that has always opened these ports in the spring to use his influence with the Minister of Railways, and have a vessel detailed for this purpose when the time is opportune.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Department of Marine and Fisheries will only be too glad to go to the rescue of the Railway Department again when the necessity arises, and detail either -the steamer Stanley or the Aranmore for the required purpose.

This increase of $320,000 seems to be a large one in these times wlhan the curtailment of expenditures is called for. Is the .increase pninioipally due to extraordinary repairs, or maintenance charges.
(Mr. BALLANTYNE: It is due to. repairs, wages, fuel, oil, and all that sort of thing. The outlay for these purposes is very much higher than in normal times, and tihat is what makes up the $320,000.
It is an increase of something over twenty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We found it absolutely necessary to put in new boilers into the Montcalm.
Are the items for repairs greater than usual?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can give you all
- the details. We have twenty-three steamers, and the repairs of the hulls and engines amount to $257,340. That embraces nearly the wlhole amount.
A few years 'ago the steamer Montmagny >was wrecked. Has any attempt been made to float her, and if so, by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
All attempts made
to raise the vessel have been quite unsuccessful. A tender was awarded to a Quebec -firm for that purpose, but, I am sorry 'to say, without any success.

What firm was given the task of floating the 'ship?
Mir. iBALLANTYNE:	I am not quite
certain; I think it was 'a company called the St. Charles Navigation lOomipany, a Quebec company.
What were the conditions of the contract which was awarded to the company in question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If the company
raised the steamer they were to pay the department $25,000, but they were unable to do so.
Then, as I understand, the Government practically sold the ship [DOT] for $25,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That would have been correct had the company accomplished the task it set out to perform.
iMr. OANNON: What time had they in which to float the ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was not any specific time, they were given a reasonable opportunity to see if they could accomplish their task, and they were unable to do so. W e now consider the contract null and void.
Mr. 'CANNON: Has any other contract been given?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No other contract has been awarded.
Has the department any intention of making further attempts to float the ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will be very glad to favourably consider any offer that is made to the department. At the moment we have not received any.

I understand that in the Quebec papers a few days ' ago it was reported that a gentleman offered to float the

Montmagny provided he received financial aid either from the citizens or from the Government. It would be a good thing for the minister to help that man if his proposition is really a serious one. The Montmagny was a beautiful ship, and it is really too bad that she should be left in the river without any attempt being made to float her, which, I understand, it would be rather easy to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it is more difficult than the hon. member appreciates, but if he will have his friends come and see me, we are open to receive offers to raise the steamer.
I have no friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry to hear that.	I
Examiners of masters and mates, $16,500.
Will the minister tell us how that $16,500 is to be expended? Do the examiners get a fixed salary, or do they receive fees from the masters and mates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The examiners get a fixed salary for the duties they perform.
Expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.

Where are those
schools located?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At St. John, N.B., Halifax, North Sydney, Yarmouth, and in the winter months they are at Quebec and Kingston.

Who looks after those
schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have no superintendent over all the schools, but we have an instructor at each one of those stations. For the city of Quebec, it is Captain P. L. Lachance.
What is his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Fifty dollars a
month.
Does he work all the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, only during the winter months.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $5,000.
I notice there is a distinct decrease in this item from the appropriation of 1917. Does the minister expect fewer obstructions in 1918 than in 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know that I do, but the department considers the
amount we are asking here will be sufficient for our needs, and we are trying to keep all the items of expenditure down to the minimum.
Mr. PARENT. Are there any particular rivers affected by this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, there is not any particular river or spot. The item covers work wherever navigation may be obstructed in any way. This vote is to remove the obstruction.
Was the amount of $20,000 for 1917-1918 all spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No.
Inspection of live stock shipments, $3,000.
What is this item for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is for live stock inspectors at the port of Montreal, Mr. Delorme, and Mr. O'Grady. Their business is to see that any live stock going aboard the steamers are properly taken care of and the necessary provision made for them.
What are their salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Delorme, $1,200; Mr. O'Grady, $1,050; miscellaneous, $750; making a total of $3,000.
Where does the live stock go to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To England-hun-dieds and thousands of horses.

Is there a station pf this kind at Quebec?
Mr. BALLANTYNE. That is not in my department; that belongs to the Minister of Agriculture.
Surely the hundreds and thousands of horses would be inspected by the British Remount Department, or the Imperial Munitions Board, or whatever department it may be which purchases these horses.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We do not inspect the horses. I would not want to convey to the hon. member the impression that we do. The business of these inspectors is to see that there are proper stalls or accommodation for horses or any other live stock that may be put on board the steamers.
The item reads, "Inspection of livestock shipments.''

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It might have been *worded a little differently.

To continue subsidy for wrecking- plants- Quebec, Maritime Provinces and! British Columbia, $35,000.
How much is given to Quebec and to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The vote is to pay the following subsidies: British Columbia Salvage Company, Victoria, $10,000; Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company, Levis, $25,000; in all, $35,000.
What service does the department get for the subsidy of $25,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is one of the matters of emergency for which the department has to provide. While I am happy to state that the St. Lawrence route below the port of Quebec, and, in fact, the whole St. Lawrence route has, practically speaking, been free from accidents, at the same time it would be unwise in the interest of navigation for the department not to. have a powerful and efficient plant ready in case an expensive steamer might come to grief.

I understand that at one time the steamer Lord Strathcona was kept constantly under steam and the Davie Company received a subsidy for this service. Is there now a boat kept under steam ready to sail at any moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Lord Strathcona is always kept under steam.
Is the Government taking over the plant that used to belong to the Davie .Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, the Government have not taken over the steamer; we are merely granting the subsidy.
I mean the wrecking plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government have not taken over the wrecking plant. The name of the company that operates it is the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company.

While I do not object to the maintenance of the wrecking plant at Levis, and while I see the necessity of it for the river St. Lawrence proper, I think it would be wise, at no distant date, for the department to establish a wrecking plant lower down the river St. Lawrence. If a wreck takes place in the gulf of St. Lawrence between Newfoundland and, say, Anticosti, or between Anticosti and Magdalen island and the bay of Gaspe, I do not wish to be parochial, but it seems to me it is too far away to send to Levis for a wrecking plant in order to meet such a contingency.

I know the department has had under consideration the erection of a wrecking plant lower down the river St. Lawrence. If the minister contemplates the erection of a plant there I might, perhaps, give him some of my own ideas aibout that. I consider the bay of Gaspe would toe the proper point at vhich to have that wrecking plant.
I suppose the hon. member is speaking now as the member for Gaspe.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The department have not under consideration at the present time the establishment of a wrecking plant toelo-w the port of Quelbec, but I shall toe glad to give the matter consideration.
Mr. TOLMIEt- Has any reduction been made in the subsidy to the British Columbia company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The British Columbia appropriation remains the same.

Many serious wrecks
occur, I 'believe, on the Newfoundland coast. To- have ready access to these, even my hon. friend's port of Gaspe would hardly be suitable. I do not want to suggest any port in my own 'constituency, 'because that would look like parochialism-, but I would suggest in all seriousness that a plant established- at Sydney or at North Sydney would be a better location for the class of wreck with which the department has to deal. It i-s worth considering at all events-, in the future planning of these arrangements-.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall toe very glad to take -into consideration the suggestions made toy my hon. friends.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I beg to move
that the Committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to s-it again this day.
Motion 'agreed to; progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The Hous£ again- in- Committee on Bill No. 3, to- confer the electoral franchise upon women, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Women to toe entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have given
consideration to some of the suggestions which were made with regard to the terms o-f this Bill, and I now propose the following amendment:
That subclauses (c) and (d) of the first subsection of section 1 be struck out and the following be substituted therefor as subclause (c) :

Possesses the qualifications which would entitle a male person to vote at a Dominion Election in the province in which said female person seeks to vote. Provided that a married woman or an unmarried daughter living with her father or mother shall be deemed to have any necessary qualification as to property or income if the husband or either of the parents is so qualified.
The reason for that amendment is that it brings the qualification for a woman for the electoral franchise more nearly in line with that which is necessary for a man. As the clause was originally drafted, it gave women a somewhat wider franchise than men.
Has the Bill been reprinted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, that is the reason I am moving these amendments now. The object of the subsection in the first place, is to provide that the qualification of women shall be the same as that which would entitle a male person to vote at a Dominion election in the province in which the woman seeks to vote, but inasmuch as that provision, if unaccompanied by any qualification, would cut out a very large number of women from the right to vote, where that right is based upon property or income, therefore the clause goes on to provide:
That a married woman or an unmarried daughter living with her father or mother shall be deemed to have any necessary qualification as to property or income If the husband or either of the parents is so qualified.
That amendment removes the difficulty which was suggested as to the term of residence in the Bill as originally drafted. It is proper that hon. members should have time to consider the amendment, so I will ask that it stand. I also beg to move:
That subclause (c) of the second subsection of section 1 be amended by striking out the words ''being a married woman and previously an alien," in first line thereof, and by substituting the word "parent" for the word "father," in the third line thereof, and by inserting after the word "constituency," in the ninth line thereof, the words "while he is so engaged in such preparation or revision. '
The clause will then read:
If she has become a British subject by marriage or by the naturalization as a British subject of her parent while she was a minor and in either case has done nothing (other than in the second case by marriage) to forfeit or lose her status as a British subject, and obtains and presents to the official in charge of the preparation or revision of the voters' lists of the said constituency, while he is so engaged in such preparation or revision, a certificate under the signature of a judge,-
And so on. I also give notice that I will move that the second section be amended by adding thereto the following at the end thereof:
And in each of the said Acts the expression "person" or "male person" or any similar expression, shall include a female person, unless a different meaning is required by the context, or by the terms of this Act.
As far as I can judge, these amendments will cover such of the objections as were urged on a previous occasion, in so far as seems desirable to give effect to any suggestion so made.
When will these amendments come up for consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Just as soon as we can take them up.
Will the Bill be reprinted for to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope so.
Do I understand the principle of the Bill will be discussed in Committee of the Whole, when it is taken up again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The principle of a Bill is always discussed on the second reading.

I understood that we passed over the Bill rather lightly on the second reading, because an understanding had been reached between the leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister that there might be fuller discussion either in Committee of the Whole or on the third reading. The object was to give members more time to go into details of the Bill, and study it more closely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The principle of a Bill is one thing and the details another. I do not recall any understanding that the principle was to be discussed in committee. It is not usual to discuss the principle of a Bill in committee. The principle is discussed on the second reading and the details are discussed in committee, but if my hon. friend desires to relieve his mind of any view as to the principle of the Bill, perhaps we might waive the rules for the time being and let him have the opportunity.

I do not want any favour in that regard, but I understood at the time that we suspended the discussion on the second reading with 'the distinct understanding that there would be a general discussion in Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not recall it; it may be so.

On page 98 of Hansard I find:
Sir Robert Borden: In order to make the matter perfectly clear, permit me to say that we are merely carrying out in this respect, the same principles with regard to women which now prevail in regard to men.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I do not intend to
discuss the principle of the Bill on the present occasion, but will reserve any remarks I may have to make on that subject.
I told some bon. gentlemen who were inquiring about the matter that my understanding was that those who had any remarks to make on the principle of the Bill would be given, an opportunity to make them when the Bill came up in Committee of the Whole, the same as on, a second reading.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would not
understand that the observation to which my bon. friend has called attention would constitute any such understanding as he suggests, but, as I said before, I have no desire to be strict in the enforcement of the rules. It would be undesirable, I think, to have a protracted discussion in committee on the principle of the Bill, when the principle should be discussed on the second reading, if at all.

On page 97 of Hansard I find:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: The House is very thin at the moment, and I do not purpose to discuss the principle of the Bill at this stage, as I understand several members wish to speak on it. I suggest that we give the Bill its second reading and go into Committee upon it, when the information I desire can better be given than across the floor of the House.
Of course I understand the hon. minister would not prevent any one discussing the principle of the Bill, because he tacitly agreed that the principle of the Bill would be discussed in committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will not admit that I tacitly agreed to anything. However, I do not think we will have any trouble.

I understood the other day that this Bill would come before the committee again and be examined on its merits. If the minister is ready to hear discussion on the subject at once I am prepared to go on. Otherwise, I would have to wait until a future time, when the matter will come up for discussion. I may say I am opposed to the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think we had better go out of committee now, without prejudice to any rights my hon. friend had.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivirr' in the Chair. -
Ocean and River Service-Unforeseen expenses, $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
While we are asking for a vote of $5,000, I wish to inform hon. gentlemen that the expenditure up to February 28, 1918, only amounted to $64.05, but we thought it wise to ask for a vote of $5,000, although I do not think we will spend any more next year than we did last year.
Amount required for two boilers for Canadian Government Steamer Montcalm, $60,000.
Is it the minister's intention to call for tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is the intention of the department to put in a similar make of boilers-, BaibcoCk & Wilcox, if we can get it at a reasonable sum. If we are unable to do-so we will call for public tender.

I understand the intention of the department at present is not to call for tenders.
Amount required for two steamers for buoy service in Maritime provinces, $300,000.

Is it- the intention
of the department to purchase two new steamers to replace two that are at the present time in use or is it intended to add two new steamers to the fleet?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The intention is to add two new steamers. Unfortunately the department lost several boats; the Mont-magny was one 'and there was also the unfortunate foundering of the steamer Simcoe. The intention is to -build two new steamers especially designed for carrying buoys and for the service which 'they may he called upon 'to perform.
My hon. friend has referred to the Simcoe. That was a very sad accident. Has an investigation disclosed anything as to the cause of that accident?

Was the steamer Simcoe insured, and if so, for how much? I would like also to ask if the department has investigated the possibility of salvaging that boat?
iM.r. BALLANTYNE:	The Government
carry their own insurance. This steamer

was not covered by insurance in any outside company. We have not been able to salvage the steamer although we have endeavoured to do so.
Mr. LEM'IEUX:	Will the minister give
me the information about 'the Simcoe?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was no formal investigation held, but a very thorough inquiry was made by the department.
I regret to inform t'he commSttee that we have no information that would enable us to tell what was the cause of the loss.

How many people
perished?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I aim sorry I have
not the exact number, hut I think it was 42.
Are the ships going to be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly; it is the
policy of the Canadian Government to have everything built in Canada.
[Mr. CANNON: Has the construction of these ships started?
'Mr. BALLANTYNE:	No, not yet; we
would not care to do that without the approval of hon. members and the House generally.

Is there any vote
for new buoys?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This particular
vote we are asking for is not for buoys. It is for two new 'steamers to he used in placing buoys.
Where are the steamers going to he built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I could not answer the hon. member because we will have to call for tenders according to the specifications of the department and whoever gives us- the lowest hid and. can turn out the best steamer will be awarded the contract.
Is it the intention of the Government to have shipbuilding plants of their own?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter has not been considered, 'by the Government, but if they ask the advice of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I may say that I will certainly he against it.
Public Works-Chargeable to capital (Marine Department)-River St. Lawrence ship ohatmel, $478,000.

Would my hon. friend
give an outline of the work to be done this
summer on the ship channel in the river St. Lawrence, and state what depth of channel they have attained and what remains to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The river St. Lawrence ship channel extends from the city of Montreal to what is known as the "Traverse," 60 miles 'below Quebec. The entire length of the channel is 220 miles. With the exception of 1.74 miles at cap a la Roche and St. Augustine bar, there is a 30-foot channel from Montreal to the sea. At cap a la Roche and St. Augustine bar advantage is taken of the rise in tide. At cap a la Roche there is a rise in tide of from 4 to 6 feet and at St. Augustin bar of approximately 13 feet. The narrowest point in the channel is at St. Croix bar. At this point the width is 250 feet. The width of the channel to the rock cut at cap a la Roche is 300 feet, which is being widened to 550 feet. The channel through lake St. Peter is 450 feet wide at the straight parts and from 600 to 800 feet on the curve. Work on the 35-foot channel has been completed over a distance of 39.90 miles. There remains yet to 'be dredged to a depth of 35 feet, 50.48 miles.
How many dredges are there under the control of the department engaged on the work in connection with this, ship channel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Owing to the financial situation we are curtailing very much the expenditure on the work to be done on the St. Lawrence ship channel this coming yeaT. We only have four elevator dredges with tugs and two self-propelling steel elevator dredges with tugs, six in all. Hon. gentlemen will notice that there is a decrease, as compared with last year, of $194,000.
Mr. LEM'IEUX:	Have there 'been any
accidents in the channel during the last fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am happy to say there have been only minor accidents^- nothing of a grave character.

Will my hon. friend
induce the insurance people to reduce their rates now that the ship channel in the river St. Lawrence is in such good order and as there are only minor accidents? Unfortunately, a few bad accidents some years ago gave Lloyds a pretext to raise their rates abnormally. I think my hon. friend, who is au fait with the navigation of the St. Lawrence, who has been vice president of the harbour commission and was con-

sequently in touch with all the oceanic interests, might endeavour to make his influence felt with that famous insurance concern and see that the rates between Great Britain and Canada under ordinary conditions are lowered. There is no reason why the river St. Lawrence should not be navigated as well as the ocean itself, with the remarkable improvement which we have witnessed in the ship channel in the last twenty years. I know that I am voicing the sentiments not only of the business community in Montreal, but of all Canada. It is a big 'question which affects not only the merchants and shippers in Montreal, but the farmers in itbe West. I hope that my hon. friend, business man as he is, will see to it that we get from Lloyds proper rates for our ocean tonnage.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can, sympathize with the hon. member's views, regarding the high rates of insurance on the St. Lawrence route. It is a matter that I gave a great deal of thought and attention to in the six years that I was one of the harbour commissioners of the port of Montreal. It is a very difficult problem, as the hon. member has stated. At the first opportune time, I certainly will take it up with the Lloyds people, because I do not know of any route that is safer, either by night or day, than the St. Lawrence ship channel from Montreal to the sea. It is thoroughly well buoyed and splendidly lighted, and the depth of the channel is now 30 feet to the sea, and in some parts 35 feet.
And the curves have been reduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. I quite agree with the hon. member that we should have lower rates of insurance, and I shall look into the matter. I do not say that I shall accomplish it, but I will make the attempt to do so. '
Is the dredging work done by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, the dredging of the St. Lawrence ship channel for many years has been done by the department's own dredges and its own staff, and that is still the policy.
Wlhere will the dredging be done next summer, at Montreal or Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The principal dredging will be done at cap a la Roche, and at St. Augustin bar, also in the north channel.
Does this item cover the dredging work in the St. Charles river?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am very happy to say that it does not. That work comes under the Public Works Department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this item carry? Carried.
Does this item also cover the lighting of the ship canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Simply the dredging.
What was the amount expended last year for dredging?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg to call the hon. member's attention to the fact that the item on dredging has been carried. If hon. gentlemen wish to ask questions, they must not wait until after the item has been declared carried.
I believe I rose before the item was carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If the Chairman will allow me, I will give my hon. friend the information. Last year the amount expended was $672,000.
To provide for construction and completion of dredging plant for St. Lawrence River from Montreal to Father Point, $163,900.
Would the minister explain the difference between the item we have just voted for the St. Lawrence River ship channel and the present item for dredging plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be very glad to give the hon. member the information he seeks. The item we have just passed is for dredging the St. Lawrence ship channel. The vote we are now asking is for the maintenance of the Sorel shipyard.

What is included in the item we voted for dredging the St. Lawrence? Does it include salaries paid to the employees, coal burned, and the expenses of the work itself?
-Mr. BALLANTYNE: Yes, quite so.
Where is the dredging plant to be built? Will it be purchased in England, or built in Canada, and if so, where?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The vote that the Committee is considering at the present time is for the maintenance of the shipyard at Sorel. The amount appropriated for maintenance is $53,900, for improvement of the shipyard, $10,000; and there is also an amount tc complete a dredge that the

Canadian Vickers Company are building that will amount to $100,000, making a grand total of $163,900.
I notice that the item reads " for construction and completion."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: "Of dredging plant."
Yes. Completion implies that the work is already started.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The word " completion " refers to the dredge that the Canadian Vickers Company have under construction at the present time for the department, and which is not finished.
Was any money voted last year for the construction of this dredge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
And the amount was not sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No.
Mr. CANNON. How much was spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It appears that
there was $150,000 voted for this dredge last year, but the work was suspended on account of the war, owing to the yard being fully occupied in building vessels more urgently required. Therefore, we are asking now for a revote of $100,000.
A revote? I understand that Parliament has already voted $150,000 for the construction of this dredge. Tenders were called for, I suppose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
And the contract awarded to the Canadian Vickers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
And the work was suspended. If I understood the minister rightly, this is not new money that we are voting. We are voting an old item for the second time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
According to the
rules of Parliament, when money is voted and is not expended for the purpose it was voted for, it is necessary to come before Parliament again for a vote.
"What I want to know is whether that $150,000 has been spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, it has not.
How much of that money has been spent on the dredge? Was a contract executed when the dredge was ordered, and has the price been changed since that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Tenders were called for by my predecessor, and the contract was awarded on the 27th October, 1914. The total amount of the contract price was $833,300. There was voted in 1915-16 $500,000; in 1916-17, $325,000; in 1917-18, $150,000, and we are asking this year for $100,000.
The minister explained at first that the contract had been awarded but that the work had been suspended on account of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

In view of the information which the minister has just given us, how can the work have been suspended when nearly $600,000 of public money has been expended on this dredge? What was the money expended for?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman is afraid that this money is not going to be spent in his province.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been a certain amount of work done on this dredge, otherwise the votes would not have been passed at each session of Parliament. It is a fact, however, that the work has been suspended. I am told this was in the summer of 1915.
Is the amount asked for intended for permanent work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The vote we are now asking hon. gentlemen to pass is for permanent work. If it is continued until it is finally completed we will require this vote of $100,000, but it is for permanent work on a new dredge.

The Department of Public Works has decided not to make any expenditures in a capital way unless they are absolutely necessary, because of war conditions. Is not the same policy to be adopted by the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member will understand that this contract was awarded to the Vickers Company in 1914. It is a valid contract, and it is obligatory on the part of the Government to carry it out. By agreement between the Vickers Company and the Government, the work has been temporarily set aside since the summer of 1915, but it is quite probable that during the coming summer, and probably before then, the Vickers Company may be in a position to complete the dredge.



They cannot do so unless we secure this vote of $100,000.
Then this is a case of a contract awarded before the war began?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
The contract was awarded in October, 1914, which was after the war had broken out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cannon) is quite correct. The war broke out, as we all unfortunately know, in August, 1914, and the contract was made in October of that year.

Including the vote asked for in these estimates, the total amount required to pay for this contract is over $1,000,000. Is that on account of the enhanced value of material entering into construction, or do you intend to pay more than the contract price for the dredge, or does any part of the sum form a revote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to make it clear that my predecessor, in October, 1914, after calling for public tenders, awarded the contract for the building of this new dredge to the Vickers Company of Montreal. There have been sums of money spent on the erection of this dredge from time to time since then, but the work has been set aside, and I am now asking for a vote of $100,000 to complete the dredge.
Mr. JOS. READ: Then the dredge has been partly built and you are going on with the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Then, including the
amount asked for in this estimate, Parliament will have voted for this work over one million dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, but that amount has not been spent.
As regards the balance of the item, where is the money to be spent, and in what manner?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The maintenance of the shipyard at Sorel will amount to $53,900, and improvements on the shipyard at Sorel $10,000.
It has been rumoured for some time that the shipyard at Sorel was to be closed1. Is there any foundation for this rumour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As far as I know it is the intention of the Government to continue the Sorel shipyards, but not on as large a scale as in the past.
[Mr. Ballantyne.l

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government
has expropriated the McCarthy property and the matter is now in the bands of the Exchequer Court.

What offer has been
made by the department to the McCarthy
estate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I ami not personally aware that any offer has been made. Pos-.sibly my predecessor may have made one, but .if so, I have no record of it here, I aim sorry to say.

We do not yet appear to have obtained all the information that we are entitled to on this item as yet. If I understand the matter aright, a contract was let in 1914 for the building of a dredge, the .contract price being $833,000. We are told that in one year $500,000 was voted, the next year $325,000, last year $150,000, and this year we are asked to vote $150,000. Were all those amounts actually paid, or was any part of them paid? In other words, when the dredge is completed and- paid for, is it going to cost the country $833,000 or more than that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the dredge is finally completed, the contract price will oe $833,700. All of the moneys that have been voted in the various years have not been spent.
Amount required for converting six ship
channel tugs for salt water service, $50,000.
*
Where aie those tugs at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At the present time they are at Sorel, and as there is a great demand for tugs to be converted into seagoing ships, and as the British Government are liable to ask for them at any time, the department is asking for this appropria-

tion to convert those six channel tugs for salt water service. At the present time, they are equipped only for fresh water service.
Are those tugs to be replaced after they are sent down for salt water service ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not the intention of the department to replace those tugs providing they are used for salt water service.
If those tugs are not to be replaced, their usefulness must surely not be very great.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I assure the hon. member their usefulness is just as great as it has ever been, but owing to the curtailment of the expenditure on the St. Lawrence ship channel, as the hon. member will have noted by the appropriation, we are not requiring for dredging work on the St. Lawrence ship channel as many dredges as we formerly did. We have, therefore, those six tugs that are idle, and we think it is good policy to have them converted for service on salt water.
The object of the minister is to put condensers in them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
Lighthouse and coast service-agencies, rents and contingencies, $178,0-00.
Will the minister explain the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The increase is due principally to salaries. As hon. gentlemen know, the cost of living has advanced so very much, and we find it necessary to increase the salaries.
Who is the agent at Quebec at the present time?

speechtext: Mr. Beland.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $485,000.
Will the lightkeepers come under the provisions of the new Civil Service Act with regard to the Outside Service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
24i

I hope the minister will extend to the lightkeepers the policy which he has just enunciated with regard to marine agents and employees in the marine agencies. I believe there is no class of public servants who are so much underpaid as the lightkeepers. They are faithful servants, their duties are very important, they are subject to many hardships, and I believe that since 1870 they have not received an increase of salary. In fact many of them have to-day a smaller salary than .their predecessors had previous to 1870. The cost of living has increased, especially during the last few years. Their w-ork is harder than it was. 'The season of work has been extended; in fact, I believe this winter they had to work until the 23rd of January. Many of them have to employ help. I know the case of one lightkeeper who has a salary of $1,400. That seems to be a good salary, but the regulations of the department compel him to employ two servants whom he has- to pay and feed, and in the end those men are much better off than he is. I consider that the salaries of the lightkeepers ought to be increased before the provisions of the new Act come into force.

I wish to support what the hon. gentleman has just said with regard to the salaries of lighthouse keepers, and I would urge the minister to apply the increase also to the lighthouse keepers on the upper lakes.

I am glad to hear the minister say that the lighthouse keepers will come under the Civil Service Commission in future. I would suggest, however, that there are cases where the Civil Service Commission might take into- consideration special circumstances. I would like to cite one or two cases. In the gulf of the St. Lawrence -there is a place called Bird's Rock, one of the Magdalen- islands, a celebrated place, and a very interesting spot to visit. There is another place called Bryon island, which was the first land sighted by Jacques Cartier when he came to Canada. There are lighthouses on both these islands. Bird's rock is but a rock, but Bryon island is an island. The lighthouse keeper who is appointed at any of these places goes into exile practically for life, except that after a certain number of years he applies for superannuation, which is granted to him; but speaking generally, they take their families with them and settle there for life. I know the lighthouse keeper at Bird's rock. He took his family with him to the Rock, and there is a sad story con-

neoted with that lighthouse, as the minister knows. In .a case of that kind, where the lighthouse keeper's son has grown up to the business, has learnt telegraphy and flag signalling and all the other work connected with keeping the lighthouse, it seems to me the department should recommend to the Civil Service Commission, other things being equal, that the eldest son should succeed his father. I also know the lighthouse keeper on Bryon island. He has been exiled there now for fifteen years. There was a new lighthouse 'built at that time at the request of the navigators and of the steamship companies, and this man was appointed at my suggestion. His name is Procul Chevrier. He is an excellent and faithful servant of His Majesty, and has kept the lighthouse admirably. Now that he is full of years he resigns, and it is his desire that his eldest son should succeed him. The son has been brought up to the work of the lighthouse in that isolated spot in the gulf ' of the St. Lawrence, and I would urge the minister to recommend the Civil Service Commission, other things being equal, to give this man's son the preference in appointing a new lighthouse keeper there. It seems to me that in special circumstances such as these the department might well intervene and make a recommendation to the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The suggestions of my hon. friends for a suitable increase in salary for the lighthouse keepers and the keepers of light .ships fall on very sympathetic ears. I have under consideration at the present time, subject to the approval of this Hous-e, an increase of salary for the lighthouse keepers and for the keepers of lightships. I am sorry that the main estimates do not provide for this increase, but I intend to put in the supplementary estimates an item of $50,000 for this purpose, and I am very glad, indeed, to know that hon. gentlemen will approve the item when it comes up. There is no question but that the salaries of the lighthouse keepers, are inadequate when we take into consideration the high cost of living. This came under my notice some little time ago, and I intended to express myself in this way even if hon. gentlemen had not brought the matter to my .attention. In regard to a pension or superannuation for the lighthouse keepers, I would be very glad to give the matter consideration.
Will the hon. minister consider the suggestion I made?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am sorry I overlooked that. Hon. gentlemen will understand that ministers have no longer any authority to make appointments, or even to make suggestions, but the deputy ministers have, and I am sure my deputy, vi'ho is present to-night, will see that the name of this man is placed before the Civil Service Commission.
Mr. GAUVREAU. Is it well understood that there will be no reduction of the crews of ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no intention ot reducing the crews of ships.
Administration of pilotage, and maintenance and repairs to Steamer Eureka, $56,300.

I wish to call attention of the hon. minister to the rather exceptional situation of the apprenticed pilots in Montreal. I do not know if my information is accurate, and if it is not I wish the minister would correct me, but I understand that in Montreal no examinations have been held for the last nine years. Young men have been apprenticed for years. They are fully competent, but, on account of these examinations not being held, they cannot beqome pilots and cannot receive the salary of pilots, and these young men are in the position of either ceasing to study or work as pilots, or else practically starve. The number of full-fledged pilots in Montreal, I understand, varies between sixty and seventy. Some of them are very old and ought to be replaced, and I think it would be in the public interest if the minister would give orders for the holding of examinations immediately, so that the young men who would be successful in examinations could perform their duties as pilots during the course of the coming summer. I understand that last year the ships were so numerous on the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and the lower St. Lawrence that the number of pilots was not sufficient to take the ships from, Montreal to Quebec, and that men- who were not competent, who had not the proper knowledge of the channel or of the river, were put in charge. All this information, as I say, has been given to me from reliable sources, and if my information is not accurate, I wish to be corrected toy the minister. I would toe very glad if the minister would give us a declaration as to whether or not examinations will be held this year, so as to improve the lot of these young apprentices in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The examinations
of apprenticed pilots do not take place less there is. a vacancy on the permanent staff of pilots, commonly known as branch pilots, and while it may Ibe regrettable, as far as the young and enthusiastic apprentices are concerned, that the branch pnote live to too old an age, or live to an age that appears old and are still able to perform their duties in an efficient way, I can quite appreciate their position. I will admit there are a number of apprenticed pilots in Montreal waiting to be examined, and to pass their examinations for promotion to
branch pilots. The remainder of the statement of the hon. gentleman in regard to inexperienced pilots being put on the Toute, is, I am sorry to say, inaccurate. No one but thoroughly experienced (branch pilots are allowed to take charge of any ships, and there was certainly a* sufficient numlber of qualified licensed pilots to take charge of all the ships that navigated the St. Lawrence from, Montreal to Quebec last year.
Is there a sufficient number now?

What is the number of
branch pilots operating between Montreal and Quebec??

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
About 50. I can
give you the names.
I do not want the names. Is there any regulation as to the number of pilots that should :be on the list? Is there a maximum fixed1?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Fifty licensed branch pilots are considered a sufficient number to take care of the pilotage system.
According to the law, would the minister have authority to increase the number, if he wished to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, yes, I have the necessary authority.

I want to draw the attention of the minister to a fact connected with some of these old men who are in positions similar to the position of the pilots of Montreal. A number of men who have been doing this work do not want the young men to come up at all, and absolutely refuse to teach them the trade, and if there are young men in connection with the Montreal pilotage who are old enough and competent enough to obtain a license, I do not see why there should be any limitation. How are they limited? Is it by regulation of the pilot commission or by the pilots themselves, or is there a statutory limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Montreal pilotage system is under the direct control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and there is a departmental regulation limiting the number of pilots to fifty, but if I found that more pilots were required than that number I certainly would see that the examination of the apprenticed pilots took place, and any vacancies that occurred would be promptly filled. The hon. member who has asked the question being a sea-faring man will understand that there is a very rigid five-year course for the appren-

ticed pilots, and the apprenticed pilots are taking that course right along. A few of them have completed the term of their apprenticeship, and are simply waiting to be examined. There is no use holding the examination of the apprentice pilots unless vacancies occur.
There is a sufficient number?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite sufficient.

Following the investigation that took place at Halifax after the disaster that happened there, I remember seeing in the papers that the scope of the investigation would be extended, so that it would cover the pilotage authority in Quebec and the pilotage authority in Montreal. I am not sure if this investigation has been held in the different places. I would like to find out whether it is the intention of the department to have a change in the administration of the pilotage authority in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The pilotage systems at Montreal and Quebec are already under the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. A commission was appointed by my predecessor some years ago and an investigation was held into the pilotage systems of both Montreal and Quebec. All the recommendations, except in a few minor cases, were put into effect by my predecessor, Hon. Mr. Hazen. Since I have been appointed minister a commission has been appointed, composed of Mr. Robb, secretary of the shipping federation of Montreal, Captain Bales, who was port warden, and Captain- Harrison, of the Furness-Withy Company, Halifax; and they held a most thorough and rigid investigation into the pilotage system of the port of Halifax. The report has been completed and I hope to lay it on the table of the House shortly. The recommendation that this commission made was that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should abolish the pilotage commission of the port of Halifax, and should take the pilotage system under his control in the same way that the pilotage systems of Montreal and Quebec have been taken under the control of the minister. The necessary authority has been taken, the pilotage system of the port of Halifax is now under my control as minister, and Captain Lindsay has been appointed superintendent of pilots. Captain Lindsay is a sea-faring man holding a master mariner's certificate and has been connected with the Department of Marine and Fisheries for some years.

The commission have also visited and looked into the pilotage systems of Sydney, Louisburg, St. John, and the Miramichi. They have not as yet rendered their report, but no doubt they will do so in due course. They will then proceed to the Pacific coast and investigate the pilotage systems of Victoria, Vancouver, New Westminster and Nanaimo. I hone that when the commission have finished their investigation of these important sea ports the department will be able to put the pilotage system on a much more satisfactory basis than prevails at the present time under various local pilotage commissions.
Were the Halifax pilots under the authority or supervision of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In an indirect way, but the local pilotage commission exercised very great authority. Now that the local, pilotage system has been abolished, as minister I am assuming the responsibility and control of the pilotage system there.
Since the minister has taken control, have any measures been taken against the pilots who were held responsible for the terrible disaster which occurred in the harbour at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Since the terrible Halifax catastrophe a court of inquiry was instituted by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That court rendered its judgment, and I understand that all those who were held by this court of inquiry to be in any way blameable for the catastrophe are being dealt with at the present time before the court.

I read in the papers at the time the investigation was held that some people thought that the calamity might have been avoided if the pilot on the Mont Blanc had been able to speak with the crew on board the ship. I understand that the ship is a French ship, that the crew was French, that the pilot was English, that he could not speak any other language than English, and that there was therefore absolutely no possibility of communication between the captain and pilot of the ship as to the direction of the ship. I do not know if these are the facts, but if they are I might suggest that the minister send down to Halifax some French-speaking pilots who would take charge of French ships, in the hope that catastrophies like that might be avoided in the future.

I come from a sea-faring country, and I know a little bit about it.. If you send down from the St. Lawrence river French-speaking pilots to navigate the waters of Nova Scotia or the gulf of St. Lawrence, or any other place along the Nova Scotia coast, it would be suicidal-it would be out of the question altogether. You men from the St. Lawrence do not know anything about Atlantic navigation; you do not know anything about the game of seamanship. I am not saying this in a carping or critical spirit, but simply by way of suggestion, but I wish that you would withhold your hand from anything affecting Sydney or its pilotage system until you can get men accustomed to conditions in Sydney harbour to investigate the system that has prevailed there. Perhaps 1 am wrong in criticising. You may have used your very best judgment, but you have never steered a boat against a sou' west wind in Halifax harbour like I have done.
I know some little thing about navigation in Sydney harbour and the Cape Breton coast, and I am giving it to you now in the very best spirit and asking 'you to take the advice of some of the Cape Breton mariners as to how they would navigate that coast before you lay sacriligious hands upon the pilotage system there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member (Mr. Butts) that every consideration will be given to the suggestion which he hais made. One who has had the experience that he has informed us he has had, is at all times worth listening to, and everything that he has stated will be given very careful consideration. In answer to the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Cannon) about French pilots at Halifax, I am not in a position to know whether there are any there or not. But we all know, especially we of the English-speaking race, that the French people ispeak one language equally as well as the other, and if there are any qualified French Canadian pilots down there, and I can find them, 1 certainly shall see that they are sent.
Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $10,000.

Where are these repairs to be made to wharves, because I see on another page of the estimates, under the heading of " Public Works Chargeable to Income," a great many appropriations made for different wharves and' (breakwaters, and repairs to wharves and breakwaters, in the different provinces.

speechtext:

The Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company.
To provide for telephones at different points throughout the Dominion in connection with aids to navigation, $500.

Is that in connection with the ship channel? I understand there was a telephone system between Montreal, Quebec, and, perhaps, points lower down the St. Lawrence.
Mr. BALLANTYNE.: This vote is asked in case there may be some isolated station where we would need to install a telephone. As a matter of fact, we have never spent any money during the last three years under this vote, but it is just by way of precaution that we are asking that the amount be voted.

If, without any additional cost, the department could at isolated points like the Magdalen islands, allow the public to connect with the main line, would the department object to that? I have received many letters of late from the islanders, and as they have not telegraphic communication, and as they have to travel quite a distance, sometimes at considerable loss of time and sometimes at considerable danger crossing the lagoons on the islands, they say that if they had the privilege of a telephone line it would give them moTe comfort in carrying on their business, and would be of more convenience for the community at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The operation of
telephone lines belongs to the Department of Public Works, -and when the estimates of that department are up I am sure that the minister (Mr. Carvell) will give the matter consideration if the hon. member will bring it to his attention.

What is this particular telephone systelh for?
Mr. 'BALLANTYNE:, For isolated lighthouses.

'That fits in exactly
with the condition of things on the Magdalen islands. The Marine Department has a station on each of these islands, and it is true that there is a telephone line on the Magdalen islands. I -am not sure whether it is controlled by the Public Works or the Marine Department.

By the Public

Amount required to pay compassionate allowances to the widows, or fathers, or mothers, or dependents of the Captain and members of the crew of the C. G. S. Simcoe who lost their lives when that vessel foundered

Wall the -minister explain upon what -basis these allowances are pa-ade up? I do not w-ant the -minister to say $100 to so-and-so -and so-and-so, but on what principle are these allowances based?

speechtext:
We will deal with the officers first. There were 11 officers who lost their lives, and their dependents -are awarded $2,000 each, making a total of $22,000. Then we come to the chief p-etty officers, 13 in number. We are allowing their dependents ($1,500 each, making -a total of $19,500. We are allowing the dependents of the balance of the crew, 20 in number, -the sum of $1,000 each, making a total of $20,000, or a grand -total of $61,500.
Mr. -POWER:	The -reason I asked this
question wa,s that I would like to be informed whether there is in the -department any fixed rule with regard to -compensation for injuries, or compensation to the relatives of those who have lost their lives while in tibe service of the department.
Mr. BALLANTYNE- We have no such provision in the department, and that is the reason we are asking the committee to vote this amount now.
Mr. CO'PP:	I notice that this item is
a .provision -made for " compassionate al

lo-wa-neas to the widows, or fathers, or -mothers, or dependents of the 'Captain and members of the crew of theC.G.S. Simcoe." I understood the hon-. minister to say that this matter has been adjusted by allowing $2,000 to the dependents of the first officers, $1,500 to those of the second officers, and smaller -amounts- to- the -dependents of -the seamen. I do not 'know what the policy of the de-partm-ent is, but I -cannot see any 'particular reason why the dependents -of an officer who- has been drowned in a catastrophe sudh as this should -be entitled to any more -compensation- than the dependents of an ordinary seaman in the same vessel who suffers the same fate. It does seem to me that is an absolutely arbritary system of making compassionate allowances. Here is an officer who may be better off financially, and may not have as many dependents to care for, and yet because he happens to occupy a little higher position than one of his men, who has worked as hard, and suffered the same fate, he receives much greater consideration. It does seem to me that the principle is wrong whereby larger compassionate allowances are given to the dependents of officers than

to the dependents of the petty officers or men.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I admit that it is an arbitrary way of fixing the amount of compassionate allowance to the dependents of these unfortunate officers and men, but the only explanation I can give is that it is the usual one, and based doubtless on the difference in the standard of living. We all know that when a person receives a greater salary they usually maintain a higher standard of living, and hon. gentlemen will quite understand that we could not make the same grant to dependents of the crew as to the dependents of the officers. We are simply following the same policy that is followed in the army, where the dependents of a colonel who is killed receive a greater pension than is awarded to the dependents of officers of lower rank, or private soldiers. There is a great deal of merit in what the hon. member has stated, but it is simply a question of what rank was occupied. I cannot offer the hon, gentleman any other reason for the difference than that.	,

Perhaps nothing I can say will deter the minister from carrying out what I might term the "aristocratic" policy that has been followed by other governments as well as this, but I desire to place myself on record in a most emphatic way against such a policy as being absolutely wrong in principle. I am democratic enough to realize that a man who is out in a storm and suffers death has done just as noble and creditable service for his country as the officers or person of higher rank who were victims on the same occasion.
